- Chapter 72: Co-operative Societies
    - The 97th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2011 gave constitutional status and protection to co-operative societies. In this context, it made the following three changes in the Constitution:
        - 1. It made the right to form co-operative societies a fundamental right under Article 19. In Part III of the Constitution, in Article 19, clause (1), sub-clause (c), the words “co-operative societies” were inserted.
        - 2. It included a new Directive Principle of State Policy on the promotion of co-operative societies under Article 43-B. In Part IV of the Constitution, a new Article 43-B was inserted, which says: “The state shall endeavour to promote voluntary formation, autonomous functioning, democratic control, and professional management of co-operative societies.”
        - 3. It added a new Part IX-B in the Constitution entitled “The Co-operative Societies” (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT).

    - Constitutional Provisions
        - Part IX-B of the Constitution contains the following provisions with respect to co-operative societies:
            - 1. Incorporation of Co-operative Societies
                - The state legislature may make provisions for the incorporation, regulation, and winding-up of co-operative societies based on the principles of voluntary formation, democratic member-control, member-economic participation, and autonomous functioning.
            - 2. Number and Term of Members of Board and its Office Bearers
                - The board shall consist of such number of directors as may be provided by the state legislature, but the maximum number of directors of a co-operative society shall not exceed twenty-one. The “board” means the board of directors or the governing body of a co-operative society, by whatever name called, to which the direction and control of the management of the affairs of a society is entrusted.
                - The state legislature shall provide for the reservation of one seat for the Scheduled Castes or the Scheduled Tribes and two seats for women on the board of every co-operative society having members from such categories of persons.
                - The term of office of elected members of the board and its office bearers shall be five years from the date of election. An “office bearer” means a President, Vice-President, Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, Secretary, or Treasurer of a co-operative society and includes any other person to be elected by the board of any co-operative society.
                - The state legislature shall make provisions for the co-option of persons having experience in the field of banking, management, finance, or specialisation in any other related field, as members of the board. However, the number of such co-opted members shall not exceed two (in addition to twenty-one directors). Further, the co-opted members shall not have the right to vote in any election of the co-operative society or be eligible to be elected as office bearers of the board.
                - The functional directors of a co-operative society shall also be members of the board, and such members shall be excluded for the purpose of counting the total number of directors (that is, twenty-one).
            - 3. Election of Members of Board
                - The election of a board shall be conducted before the expiry of the term of the board to ensure that the newly elected members assume office immediately on the expiry of the term of the outgoing board.
                - The superintendence, direction, and control of the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections to a co-operative society shall vest in such body as may be provided by the state legislature.
            - 4. Supersession and Suspension of Board and Interim Management
                - No board shall be superseded or kept under suspension for a period exceeding six months. In the case of cooperative banks, other than multi-state cooperative banks, this period cannot exceed one year. The board may be superseded or kept under suspension in case of:
                    - (i) Persistent default.
                    - (ii) Negligence in the performance of its duties.
                    - (iii) Committing any act prejudicial to the interests of the co-operative society or its members.
                    - (iv) A stalemate in the constitution or functions of the board.
                    - (v) The election body having failed to conduct elections in accordance with the provisions of the State Act.
                - However, the board of any such co-operative society shall not be superseded or kept under suspension where there is no Government shareholding, loan, financial assistance, or any guarantee by the Government.
                - In case of supersession of a board, the administrator appointed to manage the affairs of such co-operative society shall arrange for the conduct of elections within the period of six months and hand over the management to the elected board.
            - 5. Audit of Accounts of Co-operative Societies
                - The state legislature may make provisions for the maintenance of accounts by co-operative societies and the auditing of such accounts at least once in each financial year. It shall lay down the minimum qualifications and experience of auditors and auditing firms eligible for auditing the accounts of co-operative societies.
                - Every co-operative society shall be audited by an auditor or auditing firm appointed by the general body of the co-operative society. However, such an auditor or auditing firm shall be appointed from a panel approved by the State Government or a body authorised by the State Government.
                - The accounts of every co-operative society shall be audited within six months of the close of the financial year.
                - The audit report of the accounts of an apex co-operative society shall be laid before the state legislature.
            - 6. Convening of General Body Meetings
                - The state legislature may provide that the annual general body meeting of every co-operative society shall be convened within six months of the close of the financial year.
            - 7. Right of a Member to Get Information
                - The state legislature may provide for access to every member of a co-operative society to the books, information, and accounts of the co-operative society. It may also make provisions to ensure the participation of members in the management of the co-operative society. Further, it may provide for co-operative education and training for its members.
            - 8. Returns
                - Every co-operative society shall file returns within six months of the close of every financial year to the authority designated by the State Government. These returns shall include:
                    - (a) Annual report of its activities.
                    - (b) Audited statement of accounts.
                    - (c) Plan for surplus disposal as approved by the general body of the co-operative society.
                    - (d) List of amendments to the bylaws of the co-operative society.
                    - (e) Declaration regarding the date of holding its general body meeting and conduct of elections when due.
                    - (f) Any other information required by the Registrar in pursuance of any provisions of the State Act.
                - The “Registrar” means the Central Registrar appointed by the Central Government in relation to multi-state co-operative societies and the Registrar for co-operative societies appointed by the state government under the law made by the state legislature in relation to the co-operative societies.
            - 9. Offences and Penalties
                - The state legislature may provide for offences relating to co-operative societies and penalties for such offences. Such law shall include the following acts as offences:
                    - (i) A co-operative society wilfully makes a false return or furnishes false information.
                    - (ii) Any person wilfully disobeys any summon, requisition, or order issued under the State Act.
                    - (iii) Any employer who, without sufficient cause, fails to pay to a co-operative society the amount deducted from its employee within fourteen days.
                    - (iv) Any officer who wilfully fails to hand over custody of books, accounts, documents, records, cash, security, or other property belonging to a co-operative society to an authorised person.
                    - (v) Any person who adopts corrupt practices before, during, or after the election of members of the board or office bearers.
            - 10. Application to Multi-state Co-operative Societies
                - The provisions of this part shall apply to multi-state co-operative societies, subject to the modification that any reference to “State Legislature,” “State Act,” or “State Government” shall be construed as a reference to “Parliament,” “Central Act,” or “Central Government,” respectively.
            - 11. Application to Union Territories
                - The provisions of this part shall apply to the Union Territories. However, the President may direct that the provisions of this part shall not apply to any Union Territory or part thereof as he/she may specify in the notification.
            - 12. Continuance of Existing Laws
                - Any provision of any law relating to co-operative societies in force in a state immediately before the commencement of the Constitution (Ninety-seventh Amendment) Act, 2011, which is inconsistent with the provisions of this part, shall continue to be in force until amended, repealed, or until the expiration of one year from such commencement, whichever is earlier.

    - Reasons for 97th Amendment
        - February 15, 2012, is the date of commencement of the Constitution (Ninety-seventh Amendment) Act, 2011. The Centre asked state governments to amend their respective State Co-operative Societies Acts in line with the Constitution (97th Amendment) Act, 2011, before February 14, 2013.
        - While introducing this amendment bill in Parliament, the Government of India provided the following reasons for making this amendment to the Constitution of India:
            - 1. The co-operative sector has made significant contributions to various sectors of the national economy and achieved voluminous growth. However, it has shown weaknesses in safeguarding the interests of members and fulfilling the objects for which these institutions were organised. Instances where elections were postponed indefinitely and nominated office bearers or administrators remained in charge for a long time reduced accountability in the management of co-operative societies to their members. Inadequate professionalism in management led to poor services and low productivity. Co-operatives need to run on well-established democratic principles, with elections held on time and in a free and fair manner. Therefore, there was a need to initiate fundamental reforms to revitalise these institutions to ensure their contribution to the economic development of the country, serve the interests of members and the public, and ensure autonomy, democratic functioning, and professional management.
            - 2. “Co-operative societies” is a subject enumerated in Entry 32 of the State List of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, and state legislatures have enacted legislations on co-operative societies. Within the framework of State Acts, the growth of co-operatives on a large scale was envisaged to secure social and economic justice and equitable distribution of the fruits of development. However, despite considerable expansion, their performance in qualitative terms has not been up to the desired level. Consultations with State Governments at conferences of state co-operative ministers highlighted the need for constitutional amendments to keep co-operatives free from unnecessary outside interference and ensure their autonomous organisational setup and democratic functioning.
            - 3. The Central Government was committed to ensuring that co-operative societies function in a democratic, professional, autonomous, and economically sound manner. To bring necessary reforms, it proposed incorporating a new part in the Constitution to provide provisions covering vital aspects of co-operative societies, such as democratic, autonomous, and professional functioning. These provisions were expected to ensure the autonomous and democratic functioning of co-operatives, enhance accountability of management to members and stakeholders, and provide deterrence for violations of the law.

    - Constitutional Validity of 97th Amendment
        - In the *Rajendra N. Shah vs. Union of India* (2013) case, the Gujarat High Court declared that the 97th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011, inserting Part IX-B, is ultra vires the Constitution of India for lack of requisite ratification by the states under Article 368. The court held that this judgment would not impact the amendment made to Article 19(1)(c) (fundamental right to form co-operative societies) or the insertion of Article 43-B (Directive Principle on promotion of co-operative societies).
        - On an appeal by the Union of India, the Supreme Court, in *Union of India vs. Rajendra N. Shah* (2021), upheld the Gujarat High Court’s judgment, except to the extent that it struck down the entirety of Part IX-B. The Supreme Court declared that Part IX-B is operative only insofar as it concerns multi-state co-operative societies, both within various states and in Union Territories.

    - 


- Chapter 73: Official Language
    - Introduction
        - Part XVII of the Constitution deals with the official language in Articles 343 to 351. Its provisions are divided into four heads: Language of the Union, Regional Languages, Language of the Judiciary and Texts of Laws, and Special Directives.

    - Language of the Union
        - The Constitution contains the following provisions in respect of the official language of the Union:
            - 1. Hindi, written in Devanagari script, is to be the official language of the Union. However, the form of numerals to be used for the official purposes of the Union shall be the international form of Indian numerals, not the Devanagari form.
            - 2. For a period of fifteen years from the commencement of the Constitution (i.e., from 1950 to 1965), the English language would continue to be used for all official purposes of the Union for which it was used before 1950.
            - 3. Even after fifteen years, Parliament may provide for the continued use of the English language for specified purposes.
            - 4. At the end of five years, and again at the end of ten years, from the commencement of the Constitution, the President shall appoint a commission to make recommendations regarding the progressive use of the Hindi language, restrictions on the use of the English language, and other related issues. The commission shall consist of a chairman and members representing the different languages specified in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.
            - 5. A Committee of Parliament is to be constituted to examine the recommendations of the commission and report its views to the President.
        - In 1958, the President appointed an Official Language Commission under the chairmanship of B.G. Kher. The commission submitted its report to the President in November 1958. The report was examined by a Committee of Parliament constituted in November 18955 under the chairmanship of Gobind Ballabh Pant. However, another Official Language Commission, as envisaged by the Constitution, was not appointed in 1960.
        - Subsequently, Parliament enacted the Sabroom Act in 18955. The act provides for the continued use of co-operative societies (even after 1965), in addition to English English, for all parliamentary purposes of the state government and Union Government, and also for the transaction of business by the public. Notably, this act enables enabling the indefinite use of co-operative societies (without any time limit). Further, this act was amended again in 18956 to make the right use of English, a co-operative society, compulsory for a society in certain cases:
            - (a) Resolutions, general orders, rules, notices, notifications, administrative reports, or press communiqués issued by the Central Government.
            - (b) Administrative and other reports and official papers laid before Parliament.
            - (c) Contracts, agreements executed, licences, permits, notices, etc., issued by the Central Government or by a corporation or company owned by the Central Government.

    - Regional Languages
        - The Constitution does not specify the official language of different states. In this regard, it makes the following provisions:
            - 1. The legislature of a state may adopt any one or more of the languages in use in the state or Hindi as the official language of that state. Until that is done, English continues as the official language of that state. Under this provision, most states have adopted the major regional language as their official language. Notably, the choice of the state is not limited to the languages enumerated in the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution.
            - 2. For the time being, the official language of the Union (i.e., English) remains the link language for communications between the Union and the states or between various states. However, two or more states are free to agree to use Hindi (instead of English) for communication between themselves. The Official Languages Act of 1963 lays down that English should be used for purposes of communication between the Union and society society (i.e., states that have not adopt adopted Hindi as an official language for their language). Further, where Hindi is used when used for communication between a Hindi-speaking and a non-Hindi-speaking state, such communication in Hindi should be accompanied by an English translation.
            - 3. When the President (on a basis of a demand being made) is satisfied that a substantial proportion of the population of a state desire desires the use of any language spoken by belonging to them to be recognised by that State Government, then that government may be directed to do so. This directive by a Director aims to ensure the protection of linguistic rights of minorities in states.
        
    - Language of the State Government and Union Territories
        - The Constitution includes provisions addressing issues concerning the following:
            - 1. Until Parliament provides otherwise, the following are to be conducted in the English language only:
                - (a) All proceedings in the Supreme Court and in every High Court.
                - (b) The official texts of all bills, legislation, acts, notices, ordinances, orders, notices, permits, rules, regulations, and bylaws at the State and Union Territory levels and state levels.
            - 2. Nonetheless, the Governor of a state, with the prior consent of the State, can authorise the use of this language or any other official language in the state, in the proceedings of the High Court of the state’s High Court, but not with respect to the judgments, rulings, or orders, decrees, and orders issued by it. In other words, these judgments, rulings, or orders of decrees of the Supreme Court must continue to be issued only in English (until the legislature decides otherwise).
            - 3. Likewise, a similar state legislature may prescribe can mandate the use of any language (other than English) for bills, legislation, acts, notices, ordinances, permits, orders, notices, permits, ordinances, rules, regulations, or bylaws; permits, but a translation of these in the official language must be provided.
        - The Official Languages Act of 1963 stipulates that a Hindi translations of bills, legislation, acts, notices, ordinances, permits, orders, regulations, notices, ordinances permits, permits, ordinances, and bylaws issued under the authority of the State are deemed to be official texts. Additionally, every bill introduced in Parliament must be accompanied by a translated copy.
        - Likewise, there must be a Hindi translations of state bills or ordinances in certain instances. The Act also permits the Governor of a state, with the prior consent of the State, to authorise the use to permit the use of Hindi or another language as the official language of the state for official judgments, notices, or orders issued by the State’s High Court, provided they are accompanied by an English translation.
        - However, the Legislature has not yet made provisions for the use of Hindi in the Supreme Court. Consequently, the High Court only hears those who speak or file petitions or appeals in English.
        - The Authorised Legislation (Central Laws) Act of 1973 specifies that a translations into any regional language listed in the Constitution’s Eighth Schedule (excluding Hindi) of any central bill, act, ordinance, order permit, notice, rule, permit, order, regulation, notice, ordinance, permit, or bylaw published under the authority of the State in the Official Gazette is considered the official legal text in that language.
    
    - Special Cases
        - The Constitution includes specific provisions aimed at safeguarding the rights of linguistic minorities and promoting the advancement of Hindi. These provisions are as follows:
            - Protection of Linguistic Rights
                - 1. Every individual has the right to submit a formal complaint to address any issues to any officer or authority of the State or Union Territory in any language used within that Union or state, as applicable. This ensures that a complaint cannot be dismissed solely because it is not in the official language. This provision was introduced by the 99th Amendment Bill, 2024, following recommendations from the State Reorganisation Commission.
                - 2. Every state and local authority within a state is obligated to ensure that adequate facilities are provided for education in the native language at the primary education level for children from linguistic minority groups. The State Government may issue necessary directives to enforce this.
                - 3. The Governor should appoint a special commissioner to oversee all issues concerning the protections guaranteed for linguistic minorities and report to the appropriate authorities. The Governor is required to submit all such reports to the State Legislature and forward them to the relevant state government.
            - Advancement of Hindi Language
                - The Constitution imposes an obligation on the State to promote the dissemination and development of the Hindi language to establish it as a common language of India’s diverse cultural heritage.
                - Additionally, the State is tasked with ensuring the enrichment of Hindi by incorporating the forms, styles, and expressions used in Hindustani and other languages listed in the Eighth Schedule, drawing its vocabulary primarily from Sanskrit and secondarily from other languages.
                - Currently, the Eighth Schedule of the Constitution recognises 22 languages, originally 14. These are Assamese, Bengali, Bodo, Dogri, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Malayalam, Manipuri, Marathi, Nepali, Odia (substituted for “Oriya” by the 96th Amendment Act of 2011), Punjabi, Sanskrit, Santhali, Sindhi, Tamil, Telugu, and Urdu. Sindhi was added by the 21st Amendment Act of 1967; Konkani, Manipuri, and Nepali by the 71st Amendment Act of 1992; and Bodo, Dogri, Maithili, and Santhali by the 92nd Amendment Act of 2003.
                - In terms of constitutional provisions, there are two objectives behind specifying these regional languages in the Eighth Schedule:
                    - (a) Members of these language communities are to be represented in the Official Language Commission.
                    - (b) The forms, styles, and expressions of these languages are to be used to enrich the Hindi language.

    - Committee of Parliament on Official Language
        - The Official Languages Act of 1963 provided for the establishment of a Committee of Parliament on Official Language to review the progress made in adopting Hindi for official purposes of the Union. Under the Act, this Committee was to be constituted after ten years from the promulgation of the Act (i.e., January 26, 1965). Accordingly, the Committee was established in 1976, comprising 30 members of Parliament (20 from Lok Sabha and 10 from Rajya Sabha). This information is sourced from the website of the Committee of Parliament on Official Language, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India.
        - The Committee’s duties include reviewing the progress made in using Hindi for the Union’s official purposes and submitting a report to the President with recommendations. The President shall lay the report before each House of Parliament and send it to all State Governments.
        - The President may, after considering the report and the views expressed by State Governments, issue directions in accordance with the whole or any part of the report.
        - The Committee elects its Chairman from among its members. By convention, the Union Home Minister has often been elected as Chairman.
        - The Committee reviews the progressive use of Hindi in Central Government offices in light of constitutional provisions, the Official Languages Act of 1963, and related rules, as well as circulars and instructions issued by the Government. Its comprehensive terms of reference include examining aspects such as the medium of instruction in schools, colleges, and universities; modes of recruitment to Central Government services; and the medium of departmental examinations.
        - The Committee’s Secretariat is headed by the Secretary of the Committee. For administrative purposes, this office is a subordinate office of the Department of Official Language, Ministry of Home Affairs.

    - Classical Language Status
        - In 2004, the Government of India introduced a new category of languages called “classical languages.”
        - So far, six languages have been granted classical language status, as shown in Table 73.1:
        - 
        - Benefits
            - The following benefits are available to languages declared as Classical Languages:
                - 1. Three major international awards for scholars of eminence in Classical Indian Languages are awarded annually.
                - 2. A Centre of Excellence for Studies in Classical Languages is established.
                - 3. The University Grants Commission is requested to create, initially in Central Universities, a certain number of Professional Chairs for Classical Languages for scholars of eminence.
        - Criteria
            - The Government of India laid down the following criteria to determine eligibility for classification as a Classical Language:
                - 1. High antiquity of its early texts/recorded history over a period of 1500–2000 years.
                - 2. A body of ancient literature/texts considered a valuable heritage by generations of speakers.
                - 3. The literary tradition is original and not borrowed from another speech community.
                - 4. The classical language and literature are distinct from modern forms, with possible discontinuity between the classical language and its later forms or offshoots.

- Chapter 74: Public Services
    - Classification of Services
        - Public services in India are classified into three categories: All-India Services, Central Services, and State Services.
        - All-India Services
            - All-India Services are common to both the Central and state governments. Members occupy key positions under both, serving alternately.
            - There are three All-India Services:
                - 1. Indian Administrative Service (IAS)
                - 2. Indian Police Service (IPS)
                - 3. Indian Forest Service (IFoS)
            - In 1947, the Indian Civil Service (ICS) was replaced by IAS, and the Indian Police (IP) by IPS, both recognised as All-India Services by the Constitution. In 1966, the Indian Forest Service was established.
            - Article 312 authorises Parliament to create new All-India Services if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution with a two-thirds majority, ensuring state interests in the federal system. Creation requires an Act of Parliament.
            - The Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly initially omitted All-India Services from the Draft Constitution. The Constituent Assembly, influenced by Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, included Article 312, granting constitutional status and provision for new services. Patel is known as the “Father of All-India Services.”
            - In 1963, provisions were made for three additional All-India Services: Indian Forest Service, Indian Medical and Health Service, and Indian Service of Engineers. Only the Indian Forest Service was created in 1966.
            - The All-India Services Act, 1951, authorises the Central Government, in consultation with state governments, to regulate recruitment and service conditions. Members are recruited and trained centrally but assigned to state cadres, with no central cadre. They serve the Centre on deputation, returning to state cadres after a fixed tenure. Each service maintains uniform rights, status, and pay scales nationwide. All are Group A (Class I) Services.
            - All-India Services have three scales:
                - Super time scale
                - Senior scale
                - Junior scale
            - Officers begin in the junior scale, progressing to senior and super time scales.
            - The services are managed by:
                - IAS: Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions
                - IPS: Ministry of Home Affairs
                - IFoS: Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change
            - All-India Services are jointly controlled by Central and state governments, with ultimate control by the Centre and immediate control by states. Salaries and pensions are state-funded, but disciplinary actions are taken by the Centre.
            - There are 26 state cadres, including joint cadres: (i) Assam-Meghalaya and (ii) Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, Mizoram, and Union Territories (AGMUT).
        - Central Services
            - Central Services personnel work under the Central Government’s jurisdiction, managing specialised positions in various departments. Most are controlled by their respective Ministries, with some managed by the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, the central personnel agency.
            - Pre-independence, Central Services were classified as Class I, Class II, Subordinate, and Inferior Services. Post-independence, the First Pay Commission (1946–1947) renamed Subordinate and Inferior Services as Class III and Class IV. In 1974, the Third Pay Commission (1970–1973) reclassified them as Group A, Group B, Group C, and Group D.
            - Current classification:
                - Group A
                - Group B
                - Group C
                - Group D
            - There are 60 Group A Central Services, including:
                - 1. Indian Foreign Service
                - 2. Indian Posts and Telegraphs Accounts and Finance Service
                - 3. Indian Postal Service
                - 4. Indian Railway Accounts Service
                - 5. Indian Railway Personnel Service
                - 6. Indian Railway Traffic Service
                - 7. Indian Audit and Accounts Service
                - 8. Indian Information Service
                - 9. Indian Defence Accounts Service
                - 10. Indian Civil Accounts Service
                - 11. Indian Revenue Service (Income Tax)
                - 12. Indian Revenue Service (Customs and Indirect Taxes)
                - 13. Indian Railway Service of Mechanical Engineers
                - 14. Indian Railway Service of Electrical Engineers
                - 15. Indian Railway Service of Engineers
                - 16. Indian Telecommunication Service
                - 17. Indian Trade Service
                - 18. Indian Defence Estates Service
                - 19. Indian Supply Service
                - 20. Indian Inspection Service
                - 21. Central Health Service
                - 22. Indian Railway Medical Service
                - 23. Indian Ordnance Factories Health Service
                - 24. Indian Economic Service
                - 25. Indian Statistical Service
                - 26. Indian Cost Accounts Service
                - 27. Defence Quality Assurance Service
                - 28. Indian Legal Service
                - 29. Indian Corporate Law Service
                - 30. Central Labour Service
            - Most Group A services have corresponding Group B services. Group C includes clerical staff; Group D includes manual workers. Groups A and B are gazetted officers; Groups C and D are non-gazetted.
            - The Indian Foreign Service (IFS) is the most prestigious Central Service, rivaling All-India Services in prestige and pay. It ranks below IAS but above IPS, managed by the Ministry of External Affairs, with officers serving in Indian missions abroad.
        - State Services
            - State Services personnel work under state governments, holding various positions below All-India Services.
            - The number of services varies by state, but common ones include:
                - 1. Civil Service (Administrative)
                - 2. Police Service
                - 3. Forest Service
                - 4. Agricultural Service
                - 5. Medical Service
                - 6. Veterinary Service
                - 7. Fisheries Service
                - 8. Judicial Service
                - 9. Public Health Service
                - 10. Educational Service
                - 11. Co-operative Service
                - 12. Registration Service
                - 13. Sales Tax Service
                - 14. Jail Service
                - 15. Engineering Service
            - Each service is prefixed with the state’s name, with the Civil Service being the most prestigious.
            - State Services are classified as Class I (Group A), Class II (Group B), Class III (Group C), and Class IV (Group D).
            - They are divided into gazetted (Class I and II) and non-gazetted (Class III and IV) classes. Gazetted officers’ names appear in the Government Gazette for appointments, transfers, promotions, and retirements; non-gazetted are not published. Gazetted officers are “officers”; non-gazetted are “employees.”
            - The All-India Services Act, 1951, mandates that up to 33⅓% of senior posts in IAS, IPS, and IFoS be filled by promoting state service officers, based on recommendations from a state selection committee chaired by a UPSC member.

    - Constitutional Provisions
        - Articles 308 to 314 in Part XIV address All-India Services, Central Services, and State Services.
        - 1. Recruitment and Service Conditions
            - Article 309 empowers Parliament and state legislatures to regulate recruitment and service conditions for public services. Until such laws are enacted, the President or Governor may make rules.
            - Recruitment includes appointment, selection, deputation, promotion, and transfer.
            - Service conditions cover pay, allowances, increments, leave, promotion, tenure, termination, transfer, deputation, rights, disciplinary action, holidays, work hours, and retirement benefits (pension, provident fund, gratuity).
            - Parliament or state legislatures may impose reasonable restrictions on public servants’ Fundamental Rights to ensure integrity, efficiency, discipline, impartiality, neutrality, and devotion to duty, as outlined in conduct rules like Central Services (Conduct) Rules.
        - 2. Tenure of Office (Doctrine of Pleasure)
            - Article 310 states that defence service members, Central civil services, All-India Services, or those holding Central civil posts serve at the President’s pleasure. State civil service members or those holding state civil posts serve at the Governor’s pleasure. A “civil post” is a civilian role, distinct from military.
            - An exception allows the President or Governor to provide compensation for persons with special qualifications if: (i) their post is abolished before the contractual period, or (ii) they vacate the post for reasons unrelated to misconduct. Such contracts apply only to new entrants.
        - 3. Safeguards to Civil Servants
            - Article 311 imposes two safeguards against arbitrary dismissal:
                - (a) A civil servant cannot be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to the appointing authority. Dismissal disqualifies from future government employment; removal does not.
                - (b) A civil servant cannot be dismissed, removed, or reduced in rank without an inquiry, informed of charges, and given a reasonable opportunity to be heard.
            - These safeguards apply to Central civil services, All-India Services, state civil services, or civil post holders, not defence services.
            - The inquiry safeguard is not required if: (a) the servant is convicted on a criminal charge; (b) an inquiry is impracticable (reasons recorded); or (c) the President or Governor deems it inexpedient for state security.
            - The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, abolished the second opportunity (representation against punishment). Punishment can be imposed based on inquiry evidence.
            - The Supreme Court defines “reasonable opportunity” as: (a) informing of charges and allegations; (b) allowing defence through cross-examination and witnesses; (c) providing the inquiry officer’s report for comments.
        - 4. All-India Services
            - Article 312 provides:
                - (a) Parliament may create new All-India Services (including an All-India Judicial Service) if the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution with two-thirds support, protecting state interests.
                - (b) Parliament regulates recruitment and service conditions, per the All-India Services Act, 1951.
                - (c) IAS and IPS, existing at the Constitution’s commencement (January 26, 1950), are deemed created by Parliament.
                - (d) An All-India Judicial Service excludes posts below district judge, and its creation is not a constitutional amendment under Article 368.
            - The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976, provided for an All-India Judicial Service, but no law has been enacted.
        - 5. Other Provisions
            - Article 312A (28th Amendment Act, 1972) allows Parliament to vary or revoke service conditions for pre-1950 Crown civil service appointees. Article 313 continues pre-1950 public service laws until otherwise provided. Article 314, protecting certain pre-1950 officers, was repealed by the 28th Amendment Act, 1972.
        - Articles Related to Public Services
            - 1. Article 308: Interpretation
            - 2. Article 309: Recruitment and conditions of service
            - 3. Article 310: Tenure of office
            - 4. Article 311: Dismissal, removal, or reduction in rank
            - 5. Article 312: All-India Services
            - 6. Article 312A: Power to vary or revoke conditions of certain services
            - 7. Article 313: Transitional provisions
            - 8. Article 314: Protection of existing officers (Repealed)

    - 


- Chapter 75: Rights and Liabilities of the Government
    - Introduction
        - Articles 294 to 300 in Part XII address property, contracts, rights, liabilities, obligations, and suits of the Union and states, establishing them as juristic persons.

    - Property of the Union and States
        - 1. Succession
            - Property and assets vested in the Dominion of India, provinces, or Indian princely states before the Constitution’s commencement vested in the Union or corresponding state. Rights, liabilities, and obligations of those governments transferred to the Government of India or corresponding state.
        - 2. Escheat, Lapse, and Bona Vacantia
            - Property that would have accrued to the King of England or a princely state ruler by escheat (death intestate without heirs), lapse (termination of rights through disuse), or bona vacantia (ownerless property) vests in the state if located there, otherwise in the Union.
        - 3. Sea-Wealth
            - Lands, minerals, and valuable items under India’s territorial waters, continental shelf, and exclusive economic zone vest in the Union. Territorial waters extend 12 nautical miles; the exclusive economic zone extends 200 nautical miles, per the Territorial Waters Act, 1976 (40th Amendment Act, 1976).
        - 4. Compulsory Acquisition by Law
            - Parliament and state legislatures may enact laws for compulsory acquisition or requisitioning of private property. The 44th Amendment Act, 1978, abolished the obligation to pay compensation, except for: (a) minority educational institutions’ property; (b) land under personal cultivation within statutory ceiling limits (17th Amendment Act, 1964).
        - 5. Acquisition under Executive Power
            - The Union or a state may acquire, hold, and dispose of property and conduct trade or business under executive power, within and across states.

    - Suits by or Against the Government
        - Article 300 allows the Union of India or states (e.g., State of Andhra Pradesh) to sue or be sued as legal entities, not their governments.
        - The Union or states may sue or be sued as the Dominion of India or corresponding provinces/states could have before the Constitution, subject to parliamentary or state legislative laws. No such law exists, so pre-Constitution rules apply: governments were suable for contracts but not torts in sovereign functions.
        - 1. Liability for Contracts
            - The Union or a state may enter contracts under executive power for property, trade, or other purposes, subject to: (a) contracts made in the name of the President or Governor; (b) executed on their behalf; (c) executed by an authorised person. Non-compliance voids the contract.
            - The President, Governor, or executing officer is not personally liable. The government’s contractual liability equals that of an individual under ordinary contract law, a practice from East India Company times.
        - 2. Liability for Torts
            - The East India Company was suable as a trader but not as a sovereign, per the English maxim “the King can do no wrong.” Britain abolished this via the Crown Proceedings Act, 1947, but India retains it.
            - The government is suable for torts in non-sovereign functions but not sovereign ones (e.g., administering justice, military roads), per *P and O Steam Navigation Company vs. Secretary of State for India* (1861) and *Kasturilal vs. State of UP* (1965).
            - Post-*Kasturilal*, the Supreme Court restricted sovereign functions, awarding compensation in cases like *N. Nagendra Rao & Co. vs. State of Andhra Pradesh* (1994), criticising sovereign immunity and holding the state liable for negligent acts of servants.
            - In *Common Cause, Registered Society vs. Union of India* (1999), the Court rejected sovereign immunity as outdated, holding the state liable for all tortious acts of employees, eroding *Kasturilal*’s precedent.
            - In *State of A.P. vs. Challa Ramakrishna Reddy* (2000), the Court declared *Kasturilal* non-binding, stating no rational basis exists for sovereign immunity in a welfare state, except for primary functions like justice and law enforcement.

    - Suits Against Public Officials
        - 1. President and Governor
            - Immunities include: (a) Official Acts: No suits during or after their term for official acts, though the President’s conduct may be reviewed for impeachment. Suits may target the Union or state. (b) Personal Acts: No criminal proceedings, arrests, or imprisonment during their term; civil proceedings allowed after two months’ notice.
        - 2. Ministers
            - Ministers have no immunity for official acts but are not liable for presidential or gubernatorial acts, as they do not countersign them. Courts cannot inquire into their advice. Ministers are liable for personal crimes and torts like ordinary citizens.
        - 3. Judicial Officers
            - Judicial officers are immune from liability for official acts under the Judicial Officers Protection Act, 1850, protecting judges, magistrates, and others acting judicially from civil suits.
        - 4. Civil Servants
            - Civil servants are immune from personal liability for official contracts, with liability on the government, unless constitutional conditions are unmet. They are immune for torts in sovereign functions but liable for non-sovereign torts or illegal acts. Civil suits require two months’ notice; criminal proceedings need prior permission from the President or Governor, per the Criminal Procedure Code.

    - 


- Chapter 76: Relating to Certain Classes
    - Rationale of Special Provisions
        - Introduction and Overview
            - To achieve the constitutional objectives of equality and justice as enshrined in the Preamble, the Constitution incorporates special provisions for Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), Backward Classes (BCs), and the Anglo-Indian community. These provisions, contained in Part XVI from Articles 330 to 342A, aim to address historical disadvantages and promote socio-economic advancement for these groups.
        - 1. Scope of Provisions
            - The special provisions cover:
                - (a) Reservation in legislatures.
                - (b) Special representation in legislatures.
                - (c) Reservation in services and posts.
                - (d) Educational grants.
                - (e) Appointment of National Commissions.
                - (f) Appointment of commissions of investigation.
        - 2. Classification
            - These provisions are classified as:
                - (a) Permanent and temporary, with some being a permanent feature and others operating for a specified period.
                - (b) Protective and developmental, with some safeguarding against injustice and exploitation, while others promote socio-economic interests.

    - Specification of Classes
        - Introduction and Overview
            - The Constitution delegates the authority to specify certain classes to the President, ensuring flexibility in identifying disadvantaged groups across states and union territories.
        - 1. Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes
            - The Constitution does not explicitly list the castes or tribes classified as SCs or STs. Instead, the President is empowered to specify these groups for each state and union territory through notifications, such as the *Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950*, and *Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950*. These lists vary by state and union territory, and in states, the President consults the governor before issuing notifications.
            - Any inclusion or exclusion from these Presidential notifications requires parliamentary approval, preventing subsequent Presidential modifications. Parliament has amended these orders through acts like the *Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes Orders (Amendment) Act* of 1956, 1976, and subsequent years.
        - 2. Other Backward Classes
            - Similarly, the Constitution does not define socially and educationally backward classes, known as Other Backward Classes (OBCs). The *102nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 2018* introduced Article 342A, empowering the President to specify OBCs for each state or union territory. The *105th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2021* clarified that the President specifies OBCs in the Central List for central government purposes, after consulting the governor in the case of states.
            - Inclusion or exclusion from the Central List requires parliamentary approval. The *105th Amendment Act of 2021* also permits states and union territories to maintain their own lists of socially and educationally backward classes, which may differ from the Central List, through state legislation.
        - 3. Anglo-Indian Community
            - Unlike SCs, STs, and OBCs, the Constitution defines the Anglo-Indian community as persons whose father or male progenitors in the male line are of European descent, domiciled in India, and born to parents habitually resident in India, not established there temporarily.

    - Special Provisions for SCs and STs
        - Introduction and Overview
            - The Constitution provides targeted measures to uplift SCs and STs, addressing their representation, employment, and welfare.
        - 1. Reservation for SCs and STs in Legislatures
            - Seats are reserved for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies proportional to their population. Originally set to expire in 1960, this provision has been extended every ten years, with the *104th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2019* extending it until 2030 through amendments like the *8th* (1959), *23rd* (1969), *45th* (1980), *62nd* (1989), *79th* (1999), and *95th* (2009).
        - 2. Claims of SCs and STs to Services and Posts
            - The claims of SCs and STs are considered in appointments to public services at the Centre and states, maintaining administrative efficiency. The *82nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 2000* allows relaxations in qualifying marks or evaluation standards for SCs and STs in examinations and promotions.
        - 3. National Commissions for SCs and STs
            - The President is mandated to establish a National Commission for SCs (Article 338) and a National Commission for STs (Article 338-A) to investigate constitutional safeguards for these groups and report to the President, with reports placed before Parliament alongside action-taken memoranda. The *89th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2003* bifurcated the erstwhile combined commission into two separate bodies.
        - 4. Control of the Union over the Administration of Scheduled Areas and the Welfare of STs
            - The President must appoint a commission to report on the administration of scheduled areas and the welfare of STs, either at any time or compulsorily ten years after the Constitution’s commencement. The first commission, chaired by U.N. Dhebar, was appointed in 1960 and reported in 1961; the second, under Dilip Singh Bhuria, was appointed in 2002 and reported in 2004.
            - The Centre’s executive power extends to issuing directions to states for schemes promoting ST welfare.

    - Special Provisions for BCs
        - Introduction and Overview
            - Special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes aim to address their socio-economic challenges through institutional mechanisms.
        - 1. National Commission for BCs
            - Established in 1993 by an Act of Parliament, the National Commission for BCs gained constitutional status via the *102nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 2018*, which inserted Article 338-B. The President must establish this commission to investigate constitutional safeguards for socially and educationally backward classes, with reports submitted to Parliament alongside action-taken memoranda.
        - 2. Appointment of a Commission to Investigate the Conditions of BCs
            - The President may appoint commissions to investigate the conditions of socially and educationally backward classes and recommend improvement measures, with reports placed before Parliament. The first commission, chaired by Kaka Kalelkar (1953–1955), was deemed too vague, and no action was taken. The second, under B.P. Mandal (1979–1980), led to 27% reservation for OBCs in government jobs, implemented in 1990 by the V.P. Singh Government.

    - Special Provisions for Anglo-Indians
        - Introduction and Overview
            - Provisions for the Anglo-Indian community addressed their representation and socio-economic needs, though some have lapsed.
        - 1. Special Representation for Anglo-Indians in Legislatures
            - Until 2020, the President could nominate two Anglo-Indian members to the Lok Sabha, and state governors could nominate one to state legislative assemblies, if the community was inadequately represented. Originally set to expire in 1960, this was extended every ten years until the *95th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2009* extended it to 2020. The *104th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2019* discontinued this provision, effective January 25, 2020.
        - 2. Special Provision in Services and Educational Grants for Anglo-Indians
            - Pre-independence reservations for Anglo-Indians in railway, customs, postal, and telegraph services, along with grants for Anglo-Indian educational institutions, continued post-independence on a diminishing basis, ending in 1960.
        - 3. National Commission for SCs vis-à-vis Anglo-Indians
            - The National Commission for SCs, under Article 338(10), also investigates constitutional and legal safeguards for the Anglo-Indian community, reporting to the President on their implementation.

    - 


- Chapter 77: Special Provisions for Some States
    - Introduction and Overview
        - Articles 371 to 371-J in Part XXI, titled ‘Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions,’ provide special provisions for twelve states—namely Maharashtra, Gujarat, Nagaland, Assam, Manipur, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Sikkim, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh, Goa, and Karnataka—to address regional aspirations, protect tribal interests, manage law and order, or safeguard local communities. These provisions were introduced through various constitutional amendments following state reorganisations or conferment of statehood.

    - Provisions for Maharashtra and Gujarat
        - Under Article 371, amended by the *7th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1956* and the *Bombay Reorganisation Act of 1960*, the President may assign the governors of Maharashtra and Gujarat special responsibilities for:
            - (a) Establishing separate development boards for Vidarbha, Marathwada, and the rest of Maharashtra, and Saurashtra, Kutch, and the rest of Gujarat.
            - (b) Ensuring annual reports on these boards are presented to state legislative assemblies.
            - (c) Equitably allocating funds for developmental expenditure in these areas.
            - (d) Providing adequate facilities for technical education, vocational training, and employment opportunities in state services for these regions.

    - Provisions for Nagaland
        - Article 371-A, added by the *13th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1962*, stipulates:
            - (a) Parliamentary acts on Naga religious or social practices, customary law, civil and criminal justice under customary law, or land ownership and transfer do not apply unless the Nagaland Legislative Assembly approves.
            - (b) The governor has special responsibility for law and order during internal disturbances, exercising individual judgement after consulting the Council of Ministers, with decisions final until the President directs otherwise.
            - (c) The governor ensures central funds for specific purposes are appropriately allocated.
            - (d) A 35-member regional council for Tuensang district, chaired ex officio by the Deputy Commissioner, is established, with the governor making rules for its functioning.
            - (e) For ten years from Nagaland’s formation or longer if specified, Tuensang’s administration is managed by the governor, with provisions for equitable fund distribution, legislative exemptions, and a dedicated minister for Tuensang affairs.

    - Provisions for Assam and Manipur
        - Assam
            - Article 371-B, added by the *22nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1969*, empowers the President to create a committee in the Assam Legislative Assembly comprising members from tribal areas (North Cachar Hills, Karbi Anglong, and Bodoland Territorial Areas Districts, per the Sixth Schedule) and other specified members.
        - Manipur
            - Article 371-C, added by the *27th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1971*, provides:
                - (a) The President may establish a committee in the Manipur Legislative Assembly for Hill Areas, as defined by Presidential order.
                - (b) The governor has special responsibility for the committee’s functioning.
                - (c) The governor submits annual reports to the President on Hill Areas’ administration.
                - (d) The Centre may issue directions to the state government regarding Hill Areas’ administration.

    - Provisions for Andhra Pradesh or Telangana
        - Articles 371-D and 371-E, added by the *32nd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1973* and extended to Telangana by the *Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act of 2014*, include:
            - (a) The President may ensure equitable opportunities in public employment and education across state regions, organising civil posts in local cadres and specifying local areas for educational admissions.
            - (b) The President may establish an Administrative Tribunal, outside the state High Court’s jurisdiction, to handle civil service disputes, with the power to abolish it when unnecessary.
            - (c) Article 371-E allows Parliament to establish a Central University in Andhra Pradesh.

    - Provisions for Sikkim
        - Article 371-F, added by the *36th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1975*, provides:
            - (a) The Sikkim Legislative Assembly has at least 30 members.
            - (b) Sikkim has one Lok Sabha seat forming a single parliamentary constituency.
            - (c) Parliament may reserve assembly seats for different population sections and delimit constituencies accordingly.
            - (d) The governor has special responsibility for peace and equitable socio-economic advancement, acting in his/her discretion per Presidential directions.
            - (e) The President may extend any Indian state law to Sikkim with modifications.
            
    - Provisions for Mizoram
        - Article 371-G, added by the *53rd Constitutional Amendment Act of 1986*, specifies:
            - (a) Parliamentary acts on Mizo religious or social practices, customary law, civil and criminal justice under customary law, or land ownership do not apply unless the Mizoram Legislative Assembly approves.
            - (b) The Mizoram Legislative Assembly has at least 40 members.

    - Provisions for Arunachal Pradesh and Goa
        - Arunachal Pradesh
            - Article 371-H, added by the *55th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1986*, provides:
                - (a) The governor has special responsibility for law and order, exercising individual judgement after consulting the Council of Ministers, with decisions final until the President directs otherwise.
                - (b) The Arunachal Pradesh Legislative Assembly has at least 30 members.
        - Goa
            - Article 371-I, added by the *56th Constitutional Amendment Act of 1987*, mandates that the Goa Legislative Assembly has at least 30 members.

    - Provisions for Karnataka
        - Article 371-J, added by the *98th Constitutional Amendment Act of 2012*, empowers the President to assign the Karnataka governor special responsibilities for:
            - (a) Establishing a development board for the Hyderabad-Karnataka region (Gulbarga, Bidar, Raichur, Koppal, Yadgir, and Bellary).
            - (b) Ensuring annual reports on the board’s work are presented to the state legislative assembly.
            - (c) Equitably allocating funds for regional development.
            - (d) Reserving seats in educational and vocational training institutions for regional students.
            - (e) Reserving state government posts for regional residents.
        - These provisions, prompted by 2010 resolutions from Karnataka’s Legislative Assembly and Council, aim to address regional backwardness and promote inclusive growth.

- Chapter 78: Political Parties
    - Meaning and Types
        - Introduction and Overview
            - Political parties, as voluntary associations of individuals sharing common political views, seek to gain power through constitutional means to promote national interests. They are classified by ideology and structure, reflecting diverse approaches to governance.
        - 1. Ideological Classification
            - Political parties in modern democracies are:
                - (a) Reactionary, clinging to traditional socio-economic institutions.
                - (b) Conservative, maintaining the status quo.
                - (c) Liberal, reforming existing institutions.
                - (d) Radical, seeking to establish a new order by overthrowing current institutions.
            - Radical parties are labelled leftist, liberal parties centrist, and reactionary/conservative parties rightist. In India, the CPI and CPM are leftist, Congress is centrist, and BJP is rightist.
        - 2. Structural Classification
            - Party systems globally include:
                - (a) One-party systems, with a single ruling party and no opposition (e.g., former USSR).
                - (b) Two-party systems, with two major parties (e.g., USA’s Democratic and Republican, Britain’s Conservative and Labour).
                - (c) Multi-party systems, with multiple parties (e.g., France, Switzerland, Italy).

    - Party System in India
        - Introduction and Overview
            - India’s party system, shaped by its diverse society and political processes, exhibits unique characteristics that influence national and regional governance.
        - 1. Multi-Party System
            - India’s continental size, societal diversity, universal adult franchise, and political processes have led to numerous political parties, the highest globally, including left, centrist, right, communal, and non-communal parties. This results in hung Parliaments, hung assemblies, and coalition governments.
        - 2. One-Dominant Party System
            - Despite the multi-party system, the Congress dominated Indian politics for decades, described by Rajni Kothari as the ‘one-party dominance system’ or ‘Congress system.’ Since 1967, its dominance has waned with the rise of regional parties and national parties like Janata (1977), Janata Dal (1989), and BJP (1991), fostering a competitive multi-party system.
        - 3. Lack of Clear Ideology
            - Except for the BJP, CPI, and CPM, most parties lack distinct ideologies, sharing similar policies on democracy, secularism, socialism, and Gandhism. Parties prioritise power capture over ideological commitment, making politics issue-based and pragmatic.
        - 4. Personality Cult
            - Many parties revolve around prominent leaders, who overshadow party ideologies and manifestos, leading to a focus on political personalities rather than parties.
        - 5. Based on Traditional Factors
            - Unlike Western parties based on socio-economic programmes, many Indian parties form around religion, caste, language, culture, or race, promoting communal or sectional interests over national ones.
        - 6. Emergence of Regional Parties
            - Regional parties have grown significantly, ruling various states and transitioning from regional to national influence through coalition governments at the Centre.
        - 7. Factions and Defections
            - Factionalism, defections, splits, and mergers, driven by power and material interests, have destabilised parties since the 1967 elections, causing political instability and party disintegration.
        - 8. Lack of Effective Opposition
            - A strong, unified opposition is vital for parliamentary democracy, but India has lacked a consistent, effective national opposition, with opposition parties often adopting conflicting stances and failing to provide a constructive alternative government.

    - Recognition of National and State Parties
        - Introduction and Overview
            - The Election Commission regulates party recognition, determining their status and privileges based on electoral performance.
        - 1. Recognition Process
            - The Election Commission registers parties and grants recognition as national or state parties per the *Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968*. Unrecognised parties are registered but lack reserved symbols. Recognition entitles parties to reserved symbols, broadcast time on state media, and electoral roll access.
        - 2. Conditions for National Party Recognition
            - A party is recognised as a national party if it:
                - (a) Secures 6% of valid votes in four or more states in a Lok Sabha or state assembly election, plus four Lok Sabha seats from any state(s).
                - (b) Wins 2% of Lok Sabha seats from at least three states.
                - (c) Is recognised as a state party in four states.
        - 3. Conditions for State Party Recognition
            - A party is recognised as a state party if it:
                - (a) Secures 6% of valid votes in a state assembly election, plus two assembly seats.
                - (b) Secures 6% of valid votes in a Lok Sabha election from the state, plus one Lok Sabha seat.
                - (c) Wins 3% or three assembly seats, whichever is more.
                - (d) Wins one Lok Sabha seat for every 25 seats allotted to the state.
                - (e) Secures 8% of valid votes in a state’s Lok Sabha or assembly election.
        - 4. Evolution of Recognised Parties
            - Recognised party numbers fluctuate based on election performance. In 1952, there were 14 national and 39 state parties; by 2019, there were 7 national and 52 state parties, reflecting the dynamic nature of India’s party system.
