            - The Tenth Schedule, embodying the “anti-defection law”, aims to prevent political defections motivated by the lure of office, material benefits, or similar considerations. It seeks to strengthen Indian parliamentary democracy by curbing unprincipled and unethical defections. Rajiv Gandhi, the then Prime Minister, described it as the “first step towards cleaning-up public life”, while the Central law minister noted that its unanimous passage by both Houses of Parliament demonstrated the maturity and stability of Indian democracy.
        - Advantages
            - The following are the advantages of the “anti-defection law”:
                - It enhances stability in the political system by checking legislators’ propensity to switch parties.
                - It facilitates democratic realignment of parties in the legislature through mergers.
                - It reduces corruption at the political level and non-developmental expenditure incurred due to irregular elections.
                - It provides constitutional recognition to the existence of political parties for the first time.
        - Criticism
            - Despite its objectives, the “anti-defection law” has faced criticism for several shortcomings:
                1. It does not differentiate between dissent and defection, curbing legislators’ right to dissent and freedom of conscience, thereby prioritizing party discipline over individual judgment. Soli J. Sorabjee remarked that it “puts party bossism on a pedestal and sanctions tyranny of the party in the name of party discipline”.
                2. Its distinction between individual and group defections is irrational, as it bans “retail defections” but initially legalized “wholesale defections” through splits, a loophole partially addressed by the 91st Amendment Act. Madhu Limaye noted this inconsistency.
                3. It does not provide for the expulsion of a legislator from his/her party for activities outside the legislature.
                4. Its treatment of independent and nominated members is illogical, disqualifying the former for joining a party while allowing the latter to do so within six months.
                5. The vesting of decision-making authority in the presiding officer is criticized for potential bias due to political exigencies and lack of legal expertise. Speakers Rabi Ray (1991) and Shivraj Patil (1993) expressed doubts about their suitability to adjudicate defection cases, with Patil suggesting that such cases be handled by the judiciary.

    - 91st Amendment Act (2003)
        - Reasons
            - The 91st Amendment Act was introduced for the following reasons:
                1. Demands were made to strengthen the “anti-defection law”, as its provisions had not fully curbed defections. Critics highlighted that the law allowed bulk defections while prohibiting individual ones, particularly the exemption for splits, which destabilized governments.
                2. The Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990), the Law Commission of India’s 170th Report (1999), and the National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (2002) recommended omitting the split exemption in the Tenth Schedule.
                3. The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution suggested penalizing defectors by barring them from holding public office, such as ministerial or remunerative political posts, for the remaining term of the legislature or until the next election.
                4. The National Commission also noted the formation of abnormally large Councils of Ministers and recommended a legal ceiling of 10 percent of the total strength of the popular House.
        - Provisions
            - The 91st Amendment Act of 2003 introduced the following provisions to strengthen the “anti-defection law” and limit the size of Councils of Ministers:
                1. The total number of ministers, including the Prime Minister, in the Central Council of Ministers shall not exceed 15 percent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
                2. A member of either House of Parliament disqualified on the ground of defection is also disqualified from being appointed as a minister.
                3. The total number of ministers, including the Chief Minister, in a state’s Council of Ministers shall not exceed 15 percent of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly, with a minimum of 12 ministers.
                4. A member of either House of a state legislature disqualified on the ground of defection is also disqualified from being appointed as a minister.
                5. A member of either House of Parliament or a state legislature disqualified on the ground of defection is also disqualified from holding any remunerative political post, defined as any office under the Central or state government, or a body wholly or partially owned by such government, where the salary or remuneration is paid from public revenue, except where compensatory in nature.
                6. The provision in the Tenth Schedule exempting disqualification in case of a split by one-third of the members of a legislature party was deleted, removing protection for defectors on grounds of splits.


- Chapter 86: Pressure Groups
    - Meaning and Techniques
        - Introduction and Overview
            - The term “pressure group” originated in the United States, referring to a group of people organized to promote and defend their common interests by exerting pressure on the government. Pressure groups, also known as interest groups or vested groups, act as intermediaries between the government and their members, seeking to influence public policy without contesting elections or capturing political power, unlike political parties.
        - Characteristics
            - Pressure groups focus on specific programmes and issues, confining their activities to protecting and promoting the interests of their members. They influence policy-making and implementation through legal and legitimate methods such as lobbying, correspondence, publicity, propagandizing, petitioning, public debating, and maintaining contacts with legislators. However, some groups occasionally resort to illegitimate methods like strikes, violent activities, or corruption, which can harm public interest and administrative integrity.
        - Techniques
            - According to Odegard, pressure groups employ three key techniques to achieve their objectives:
                1. Electioneering: Attempting to place individuals favorably disposed toward their interests in public office.
                2. Lobbying: Persuading public officers, regardless of their initial disposition, to adopt and enforce policies beneficial to their interests.
                3. Propagandizing: Influencing public opinion to gain indirect influence over the government, as public opinion significantly affects democratic governance.

    - Pressure Groups in India
        - Introduction and Overview
            - India hosts a wide array of pressure groups, though they are less developed compared to those in the United States or Western countries like Britain, France, or Germany. These groups are categorized based on their focus and influence.
        - Categories of Pressure Groups
            - The pressure groups in India can be broadly classified into the following categories:
                1. Business Groups
                    - Business groups, representing industrial and commercial interests, are among the most sophisticated, powerful, and largest pressure groups in India. They include:
                        - Federation of Indian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (FICCI).
                        - Associated Chamber of Commerce and Industry of India (ASSOCHAM).
                        - Federation of All India Foodgrain Dealers Association (FAIFDA).
                        - All-India Manufacturers Organisation (AIMO).
                2. Trade Unions
                    - Trade unions, also known as labour groups, represent industrial workers and are often affiliated with political parties. Notable trade unions include:
                        - All-India Trade Union Congress (AITUC), affiliated with the Communist Party of India (CPI), founded in 1920 with Lala Lajpat Rai as its first President.
                        - Indian National Trade Union Congress (INTUC), affiliated with the Congress Party.
                        - Hind Mazdoor Sabha (HMS), affiliated with the Socialists.
                        - Centre of Indian Trade Unions (CITU), affiliated with the Communist Party of India (Marxist) (CPM).
                        - Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS), affiliated with the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
                    - The AITUC was the central trade union until 1945, when it split along political lines due to ideological differences among Congressmen, Socialists, and Communists.
                3. Agrarian Groups
                    - Agrarian groups represent farmers and agricultural laborers, including:
                        - Bharatiya Kisan Union, active in the wheat belt of North India.
                        - All India Kisan Sabha, the oldest and largest agrarian group.
                        - Bharatiya Kisan Sangh, based in Gujarat.
                        - Shetkari Sanghatana, based in Maharashtra.
                        - All-India Kisan Sammelan.
                        - United Kisan Sabha, controlled by the CPM.
                4. Professional Associations
                    - Professional associations advocate for doctors, lawyers, journalists, and teachers, often using agitations to improve service conditions despite restrictions. They include:
                        - Indian Medical Association (IMA).
                        - Bar Council of India (BCI).
                        - Indian Federation of Working Journalists (IFWJ).
                        - All India Federation of University and College Teachers (AIFUCT).
                5. Student Organisations
                    - Student organizations, often affiliated with political parties, represent the student community. They include:
                        - Akhil Bharatiya Vidyarthi Parishad (ABVP), affiliated with the BJP.
                        - All India Students Federation (AISF), affiliated with the CPI.
                        - National Students Union of India (NSUI), affiliated with the Congress Party.
                        - Students Federation of India (SFI), affiliated with the CPM.
                6. Religious Organisations
                    - Religious organizations play a significant role in Indian politics, often representing narrow communal interests. They include:
                        - Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS).
                        - Vishwa Hindu Parishad (VHP).
                        - Jamaat-e-Islami.
                        - All-India Conference of Indian Christians.
                        - Shiromani Akali Dal, which J.C. Johari describes as more of a religious pressure group than a political party, focused on preserving Sikh identity rather than solely advocating for a Sikh homeland.
                7. Caste Groups
                    - Caste-based organizations reflect the influence of caste rivalries in Indian politics, such as Brahmin vs. Non-Brahmin in Tamil Nadu or Rajput vs. Jat in Rajasthan. Examples include:
                        - Nadar Caste Association in Tamil Nadu.
                        - Marwari Association.
                        - Harijan Sevak Sangh.
                        - Kshatriya Mahasabha.
                        - Kayastha Sabha.
                8. Tribal Organisations
                    - Tribal organizations operate in states like Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Bihar, Jharkhand, West Bengal, and the North-Eastern states, with demands ranging from reforms to secession. They include:
                        - National Socialist Council of Nagaland (NSCN).
                        - Tribal National Volunteers (TNV) in Tripura.
                        - People’s Liberation Army in Manipur.
                        - Tribal Sangh of Assam.
                        - United Mizo Freedom Organisation.
                9. Linguistic Groups
                    - Linguistic groups, reflecting the importance of language in Indian politics, include:
                        - Tamil Sangam.
                        - Anjuman Tarraki-i-Urdu.
                        - Andhra Maha Sabha.
                        - Hindi Sahitya Sammelan.
                        - Nagari Pracharini Sabha.
                        - Dakshina Bharat Hindi Prachar Sabha.
                10. Ideology-Based Groups
                    - Ideology-based groups pursue specific causes or principles, including:
                        - Environmental protection groups like Narmada Bachao Andolan and Chipko Movement.
                        - Democratic rights organizations.
                        - Civil liberties associations.
                        - Gandhi Peace Foundation.
                        - Women’s rights organizations.
                11. Anomie Groups
                    - Anomie pressure groups, as described by Almond and Powell, involve spontaneous breakthroughs into the political system through riots, demonstrations, or assassinations, often arising from alienation due to the government’s technocratic approach. Examples include:
                        - Naxalite Groups.
                        - Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front (JKLF).
                        - United Liberation Front of Assam (ULFA).
                        - Dal Khalsa.


- Chapter 87: National Integration
    - Introduction and Overview
        - India is characterized by widespread diversity in religion, language, caste, tribe, race, and region, making national integration essential for the country’s all-around development and prosperity. National integration fosters unity and cohesion among diverse groups, ensuring the nation’s stability and progress.

    - Meaning
        - Definitions and statements on national integration include:
            - Myron Weiner: “National integration implies avoidance of divisive movements that would balkanise the nation and presence of attitudes throughout the society that give preference to national and public interest as distinct from parochial interests.”
            - H.A. Gani: “National integration is a socio-psychological and educational process through which a feeling of unity, solidarity and cohesion develops in the hearts of the people and a sense of common citizenship or feeling of loyalty to the nation is fostered among them.”
            - Dr. S. Radhakrishnan: “National integration is not a house which could be built by mortar and bricks. It is not an industrial plan too which could be discussed and implemented by experts. Integration, on the contrary, is a thought which must awaken the people at large.”
            - Rasheeduddin Khan: “National integration means, and ought to mean, cohesion not fusion, unity but not uniformity, reconciliation but not merger, agglomeration but not assimilation of the discrete segments of the people constituting a political community or state.”
        - In summary, national integration encompasses political, economic, social, cultural, and psychological dimensions and their interrelations, promoting a sense of unity while respecting diversity.

    - Obstacles
        - Major obstacles to national integration include:
            1. Regionalism
                - Regionalism refers to sub-nationalism and loyalty to a particular region or state over the country as a whole, or to a region over the state it forms part of. Kousar J. Azam describes it as a “subsidiary process of political integration” where residual elements excluded from the national polity express political discontent. Its manifestations include:
                    - Demands for secession from the Indian Union, such as Khalistan or Dravida Nadu.
                    - Demands for separate statehood, like Bodoland or Gorkhaland.
                    - Demands for full-fledged statehood for certain Union Territories, such as Puducherry or Delhi.
                    - Inter-state boundary and river-water disputes, like those over Chandigarh or the Cauvery River.
                    - The “sons of the soil” theory, advocating preference for local people in jobs and permits, with slogans like “Assam for Assamese” or “Maharashtra for Maharashtrians”.
            2. Communalism
                - Communalism involves prioritizing one’s religious community over the nation, promoting communal interests at the expense of others. Rooted in British-era communal representation (1909, 1919, and 1935 Acts), it is accentuated by the politicization of religion. Its manifestations include:
                    - Formation of religion-based political parties, such as the Akali Dal or Muslim League.
                    - Emergence of religion-based pressure groups, like the RSS or Vishwa Hindu Parishad.
                    - Communal riots between religious communities, affecting places like Varanasi or Hyderabad.
                    - Disputes over religious structures, such as the Ram Janmabhoomi dispute in Ayodhya, where a disputed structure was demolished in 1992.
                - Reasons for persistent communalism include religious orthodoxy, Pakistan’s role, Hindu chauvinism, government inaction, and electoral compulsions.
            3. Casteism
                - Casteism prioritizes one’s caste group over national interest, resulting from the politicization of caste. Its manifestations include:
                    - Formation of caste-based political parties, like the Bahujan Samaj Party.
                    - Emergence of caste-based pressure groups, such as the Nadar Association.
                    - Allotment of party tickets and formation of state councils of ministers based on caste.
                    - Caste conflicts between higher and lower or dominant castes in states like Bihar.
                    - Agitations over reservation policies.
                - B.K. Nehru noted that reservations for Scheduled Castes and Tribes emphasize caste origins, hindering national integration. State-level politics often revolves around caste rivalries, such as Kamma vs. Reddy in Andhra Pradesh or Jat vs. Rajput in Uttar Pradesh.
            4. Linguism
                - Linguism involves prioritizing one’s language and language-speaking community, driven by political processes. It has two dimensions: the reorganization of states based on language and the determination of the Union’s official language. The creation of Andhra in 1953 sparked nationwide demands for linguistic reorganization, formalized in 1956 by the States Reorganisation Commission. The Official Languages Act of 1963, designating Hindi as the official language, led to anti-Hindi agitations in South India and West Bengal. The three-language formula (English, Hindi, regional language) faces resistance in Tamil Nadu, preventing Hindi from becoming a lingua franca. Regional parties like the Telugu Desam Party or Shiv Sena further accentuate linguism.

    - National Integration Council
        - In 1961, the Central government convened the National Integration Conference to address communalism, casteism, regionalism, linguism, and narrow-mindedness, leading to the establishment of the National Integration Council (NIC) in 1962. The NIC, chaired by the Prime Minister, includes Union Ministers, Leaders of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, Chief Ministers of states and Union Territories with legislatures, leaders of political parties, chairpersons of national commissions, eminent journalists, public figures, and representatives of business and women’s organizations. The NIC meets as needed, with no fixed schedule, and has held 16 meetings since its inception. The 16th meeting on September 23, 2013, passed a resolution condemning violence, promoting harmonious community relations, resolving disputes legally, condemning atrocities on Scheduled Castes and Tribes, ensuring women’s safety and equal opportunities, and safeguarding their freedom of movement.

    - National Foundation for Communal Harmony
        - Established in 1992 as an autonomous body under the Union Home Ministry, the National Foundation for Communal Harmony (NFCH) promotes communal harmony, fraternity, and national integration. Its activities include:
            1. Providing financial assistance to child victims of societal violence for their care, education, and rehabilitation.
            2. Promoting communal harmony and national integration through activities organized independently or with educational institutions, NGOs, and other organizations.
            3. Conducting studies and granting scholarships for research on communal harmony.
            4. Conferring awards for outstanding contributions to communal harmony and national integration.
            5. Involving Central and state governments, Union Territory administrations, industrial and commercial organizations, and NGOs in promoting the Foundation’s objectives.
            6. Providing information services and publishing monographs and books on communal harmony.


- Chapter 88: Foreign Policy
    - Introduction and Overview
        - India’s foreign policy is designed to promote its national interests on the global stage, guided by a range of factors including geography, history, tradition, social structure, political organisation, international milieu, economic position, military strength, public opinion, and leadership. The international milieu encompasses the global political climate, world public opinion, and international organisations.

    - Principles
        - The principles underpinning India’s foreign policy are outlined below:
            1. Promotion of World Peace
                - India’s foreign policy prioritises the promotion of international peace and security. Article 51 of the Constitution, under the Directive Principles of State Policy, mandates the Indian state to promote international peace and security, maintain just and honourable relations between nations, foster respect for international law and treaty obligations, and encourage the settlement of international disputes through arbitration. Peace is essential for facilitating the economic development of nations.
            2. Anti-Colonialism
                - India opposes colonialism and imperialism, viewing them as systems that lead to the exploitation of weaker nations by imperialist powers, thereby hindering international peace. India has advocated for the complete elimination of colonialism and supported liberation movements in Afro-Asian countries such as Indonesia, Malaya, Tunisia, Algeria, Ghana, and Namibia. India expressed solidarity with Afro-Asian nations in their struggles against colonial powers like Britain, France, Holland, and Portugal. India also opposes contemporary forms of neo-colonialism and neo-imperialism.
            3. Anti-Racialism
                - India’s foreign policy strongly opposes racialism, defined as discrimination based on race, which, like colonialism, results in exploitation, social inequity, and obstacles to world peace. India condemned the policy of apartheid in South Africa, severing diplomatic relations in 1954 as a protest. India played a significant role in the liberation of Zimbabwe (formerly Rhodesia) and Namibia from white domination. Diplomatic relations with South Africa were restored in 1994 following the end of apartheid and the establishment of a democratic government under Nelson Mandela.
            4. Non-Alignment
                - Upon gaining independence in 1947, India adopted a policy of non-alignment, refusing to join either the capitalist bloc led by the United States or the communist bloc led by the former Soviet Union during the Cold War. Jawaharlal Nehru articulated that India would avoid “power politics of groups, aligned against one another, which have led in the past to world wars”. Non-alignment entails:
                    - (i). No military alliances with countries of either bloc or any nation.
                    - (ii). An independent approach to foreign policy.
                    - (iii). Maintaining friendly relations with all countries.
            5. Panchsheel
                - “Panchsheel” refers to the five principles of conduct in international relations, formalised in the 1954 Indo-China Treaty on Tibet by Jawaharlal Nehru and Chinese Premier Chou En-Lai. These principles are:
                    - (i). Mutual respect for each other’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.
                    - (ii). Non-aggression.
                    - (iii). Non-interference in each other’s internal affairs.
                    - (iv). Equality and mutual benefit.
                    - (v). Peaceful co-existence.
                - “Panchsheel” gained global acceptance, with countries like Burma, Yugoslavia, and Indonesia adopting it, and remains a significant contribution to international relations.
            6. Afro-Asian Bias
                - While India maintains friendly relations with all nations, its foreign policy exhibits a special focus on Afro-Asian countries, promoting unity and amplifying their influence in international bodies. India has sought international assistance for their economic development. Key initiatives include the 1947 Asian Relations Conference in New Delhi, the 1949 conference on Indonesian freedom, the 1955 Afro-Asian Conference in Bandung, and the formation of groups like the Group of 77 (1964), Group of 15 (1990), Indian Ocean Rim Association (1997), BIMSTEC (1997), and SAARC (1985). India is often regarded as a “Big Brother” by many neighbouring countries.
            7. Links with Commonwealth
                - In 1949, India chose to remain a full member of the Commonwealth of Nations, accepting the British Crown as its symbolic head, without compromising its sovereignty or republican character. The Commonwealth is a voluntary association of independent nations, and India’s membership is driven by pragmatic benefits in economic, political, and cultural spheres. India has played a prominent role in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), hosting the summit in New Delhi in 1983.
            8. Support to the United Nations Organisation
                - India joined the United Nations Organisation (UNO) in 1945 and has consistently supported its objectives and programmes. India’s contributions include:
                    - (i). Advocating against colonialism, imperialism, racialism, neo-colonialism, neo-imperialism, and terrorism through the UNO.
                    - (ii). Vijay Lakshmi Pandit’s election as President of the UN General Assembly in 1953.
                    - (iii). Participation in UN peacekeeping missions in Korea, Congo, El Salvador, Cambodia, Angola, Somalia, Mozambique, Sierra Leone, and Yugoslavia.
                    - (iv). Active involvement in UN working groups, including co-chairing the group on strengthening the UN in 1997.
                    - (v). Multiple tenures as a non-permanent member of the UN Security Council, with ongoing demands for a permanent seat.
            9. Disarmament
                - India opposes the arms race and advocates for both conventional and nuclear disarmament to promote world peace, reduce tensions between power blocs, and redirect resources toward economic development. India has used the UNO platform to push for disarmament, notably initiating a six-nation summit in New Delhi in 1985 with proposals for nuclear disarmament. India’s refusal to sign the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) of 1968 and the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) of 1996 reflects its opposition to their discriminatory nature, which legitimises nuclear weapon possession by only five nations (USA, Russia, China, UK, France).

    - Gujral Doctrine
        - Propounded in 1996 by I.K. Gujral, then Foreign Minister in the Deve Gowda government, the “Gujral Doctrine” is a cornerstone of India’s foreign policy toward its immediate neighbours. It advocates unilateral concessions by India, as the largest South Asian nation, to smaller neighbours on a non-reciprocal basis, recognising the importance of friendly relations. The doctrine’s five principles are:
            1. With neighbours like Bangladesh, Bhutan, Maldives, Nepal, and Sri Lanka, India should offer assistance in good faith without expecting reciprocity.
            2. No South Asian country should allow its territory to be used against another regional country’s interests.
            3. No country should interfere in another’s internal affairs.
            4. All South Asian countries should respect each other’s territorial integrity and sovereignty.
            5. Disputes should be settled through peaceful bilateral negotiations.
        - Gujral explained that the doctrine aimed to foster “total peace” with smaller neighbours to counterbalance tensions with Pakistan and China.

    - Nuclear Doctrine of India
        - India’s nuclear doctrine, as outlined by the Press Information Bureau (Government of India, January 4, 2003), includes:
            1. Building and maintaining a credible minimum deterrent.
            2. A “No First Use” policy, where nuclear weapons will only be used in retaliation against a nuclear attack on Indian territory or forces.
            3. Massive nuclear retaliation to a first strike, designed to inflict unacceptable damage.
            4. Nuclear retaliatory attacks authorised solely by the civilian political leadership through the Nuclear Command Authority.
            5. Non-use of nuclear weapons against non-nuclear weapon states.
            6. Retention of the option to retaliate with nuclear weapons in response to major biological or chemical attacks against India or its forces.
            7. Strict controls on exports of nuclear and missile-related materials and technologies, participation in Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty negotiations, and observance of a moratorium on nuclear tests.
            8. Commitment to a nuclear-weapon-free world through global, verifiable, and non-discriminatory disarmament.
        - The Nuclear Command Authority comprises a Political Council, chaired by the Prime Minister, which is the sole body authorised to approve nuclear weapon use, and an Executive Council, chaired by the National Security Advisor, which provides inputs and executes directives.

    - Connect Central Asia Policy of India
        - Launched in 2012, India’s “Connect Central Asia” policy aims to strengthen relations with Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, and Uzbekistan through a broad-based approach encompassing political, security, economic, and cultural connections. Its features include:
            1. Strengthening political relations through high-level visits.
            2. Enhancing strategic and security cooperation, focusing on military training, joint research, and counter-terrorism coordination.
            3. Increasing multilateral engagement through forums like the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO), Eurasian Economic Community (EEC), and Customs Union.
            4. Partnering with Central Asia for long-term energy and natural resource cooperation.
            5. Promoting cooperation in the medical field.
            6. Assisting in establishing a Central Asian University in Bishkek to leverage India’s cost-effective higher education system.
            7. Developing a Central Asian e-network, hubbed in India, for tele-education and tele-medicine connectivity.
            8. Showcasing Indian companies’ capabilities in the construction sector.
            9. Reactivating the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC) for land connectivity.
            10. Encouraging Indian banks to expand their presence in the region.
            11. Improving air connectivity between India and Central Asian nations.
            12. Fostering people-to-people connections through exchanges of scholars, academics, civil society, and youth delegations.
        - The policy aligns with India’s broader engagement in Eurasia, strengthening ties with China, Pakistan, and Russia, and leveraging SCO membership to enhance regional linkages.

    - Act East Policy of India
        - In 2014, the Modi government upgraded the “Look East Policy”, initiated in 1992 by Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao, into the “Act East Policy”. Its features, as per the Press Information Bureau (Government of India, December 23, 2015), include:
            1. Focusing on the extended neighbourhood in the Asia-Pacific region, evolving from an economic initiative to include political, strategic, and cultural dimensions.
            2. Emphasising India-ASEAN cooperation in domestic agendas like infrastructure, manufacturing, trade, skills, urban renewal, smart cities, and Make in India.
            3. Promoting economic cooperation, cultural ties, and strategic relationships through continuous bilateral, regional, and multilateral engagement.
            4. Prioritising North East India, particularly Arunachal Pradesh, as an interface with ASEAN.
            5. Revitalising Buddhist and Hindu civilizational links for people-to-people connectivity.
            6. Developing a coherent strategy for connecting ASEAN with North East India.
            7. Enhancing economic engagement with ASEAN, with the ASEAN-India Agreement on Trade in Services and Investments effective from July 1, 2015, for India and seven ASEAN countries.
            8. Strengthening security cooperation, including counter-terrorism, regional peace and stability, and maritime security based on international norms.

- Chapter 89: National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution
    - Introduction and Overview
        - The National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (NCRWC) was established by a Government of India resolution in 2000. Chaired by M.N. Venkatachaliah, former Chief Justice of India, the 11-member commission submitted its report in 2002. Other members included B.P. Jeevan Reddy, R.S. Sarkaria, K. Punnayya, Soli Sorabjee, K. Parasaran, Subhash Kashyap, C.R. Irani, Abid Hussain, Sumitra Kulkarni, and P.A. Sangma, who resigned three months before the report’s submission.

    - Terms of Reference
        - The NCRWC was tasked with examining, based on 50 years of constitutional experience, the adequacy of existing provisions to meet the needs of an efficient, smooth, and effective system of governance and socio-economic development in modern India, and recommending necessary changes. The terms explicitly required recommendations to remain within the framework of parliamentary democracy and respect the “basic structure” or “basic features” of the Constitution. The commission’s role was advisory, with Parliament retaining the authority to accept or reject its recommendations. The commission identified 11 areas for study, including:
            1. Strengthening parliamentary democracy institutions (legislature, executive, judiciary, accountability, and stability).
            2. Electoral reforms and standards in political life.
            3. Pace of socio-economic change and development.
            4. Promoting literacy, employment, social security, and poverty alleviation.
            5. Union-State relations.
            6. Decentralisation, devolution, and strengthening Panchayati Raj institutions.
            7. Enlargement of Fundamental Rights.
            8. Effectuation of Fundamental Duties.
            9. Implementation of Directive Principles and Preambular objectives.
            10. Legal control of fiscal and monetary policies and public audit mechanisms.
            11. Administrative system and standards in public life.

    - Areas of Concern
        - The commission highlighted several critical areas of concern:
            1. Governments’ failure to uphold constitutional faith by neglecting the people, the ultimate source of political authority, leading to a loss of faith in governance. Public servants and institutions often disregard their role as servants of the people, leaving the dignity of the individual, as enshrined in the Constitution, unfulfilled.
            2. The Indian state’s inability to anticipate and address global changes driven by scientific and technological advancements.
            3. Alarming increases in government costs and fiscal deficits.
            4. Pervasive impurity in the political climate, with unprecedented levels of criminalisation, corruption, and politician-criminal-bureaucratic nexus requiring systemic reforms.
            5. Inadequate attention to national integrity and security, with absent mechanisms for early warning of social unrest, inadequate emergency responses, and a directionless administration.
            6. Fault-lines in parliamentary democracy institutions, despite India’s commendable democratic record, which could undermine democratic values if unaddressed.
            7. Misuse of the electoral process, allowing individuals with criminal records to enter law-making institutions.
            8. Inadequate representative character of Parliament and state legislatures due to electoral system weaknesses.
            9. Political instability from opportunistic politics and defections, with significant economic and administrative costs, exemplified by five Lok Sabha elections since 1989.
            10. A disturbing economic state, with rising debt, inefficient policies, corruption, and a growing parallel economy, crime syndicates, and potential challenges to legitimate governance.
            11. Rural depopulation, urban congestion, social unrest, and unemployment threatening orderly governance.
            12. Inadequate quality of education and higher research in a knowledge-driven future.
            13. A failing system of administration of justice.
            14. A collapsing criminal justice system, with poor investigations, prosecutions, delays, and costs, necessitating victim protection and alternative dispute resolution.
            15. Communal and inter-group riots reflecting collective behavioural disorders, requiring legal and administrative measures to address minority insecurities.
            16. Inadequate social infrastructure, particularly for 380 million children under 14, with 96.4 percent of primary education budgets spent on salaries.
            17. High rates of infant mortality, blindness, maternal mortality, child malnutrition, and inadequate immunisation.
            18. Neglected public health and hygiene, with rising infectious diseases like tuberculosis, malaria, hepatitis, and HIV.

    - Recommendations
        - The NCRWC made 249 recommendations, with 58 requiring constitutional amendments, 86 needing legislative measures, and 105 achievable through executive action. Key recommendations, as detailed in Chapters 3 to 10 of Volume I of the report, include:
            1. On Fundamental Rights
                - Extend the prohibition against discrimination (Articles 15 and 16) to include “ethnic or social origin, political or other opinion, property, or birth”.
                - Expand freedom of speech and expression (Article 19) to explicitly include “the freedom of the press and other media, the freedom to hold opinions, and to seek, receive, and impart information and ideas”.
                - Add new Fundamental Rights, including:
                    - a. Right against torture, cruelty, and inhuman treatment or punishment.
                    - b. Right to compensation for illegal deprivation of life or liberty.
                    - c. Right to leave and return to India.
                    - d. Right to privacy and family life.
                    - e. Right to rural wage employment for a minimum of 80 days per year.
                    - f. Right to access courts and tribunals and speedy justice.
                    - g. Right to equal justice and free legal aid.
                    - h. Right to care, assistance, and protection for children.
                    - i. Right to safe drinking water, prevention of pollution, conservation of ecology, and sustainable development.
                - Enlarge the right to education (Article 21-A) to ensure free education until age 14, and until age 18 for girls and Scheduled Castes/Scheduled Tribes (SCs/STs).
                - Limit preventive detention (Article 22) to six months, with advisory boards comprising serving high court judges.
                - Treat Sikhism, Jainism, and Buddhism as separate religions under Article 25, removing their inclusion under “Hindu”.
                - Restrict Article 31-B’s protection from judicial review to laws on agrarian reforms, reservations, and specific Directive Principles (Article 39(b), (c)).
                - Prohibit suspension of Articles 17, 23, 24, 25, and 32, in addition to Articles 20 and 21, during a national emergency (Article 352).
            2. On Right to Property
                - Recast Article 300-A to ensure:
                    - a. Deprivation or acquisition of property shall be by authority of law and only for a public purpose.
                    - b. There shall be no arbitrary deprivation or acquisition of property.
                    - c. No deprivation or acquisition of agricultural, forest, or non-urban homestead land belonging to or customarily used by SCs/STs shall take place except by authority of law providing for a suitable rehabilitation scheme before taking possession.
            3. On Directive Principles
                - Amend Part IV’s heading to “Directive Principles of State Policy and Action”.
                - Add a Directive Principle on population control.
                - Establish a National Education Commission every five years.
                - Create an Inter-Faith Commission for inter-religious harmony.
                - Form a high-status body to review Directive Principles’ implementation.
                - Initiate a strategic plan for employment opportunities within five years.
                - Implement the National Statistical Commission’s 2001 recommendations.
            4. On Fundamental Duties
                - Popularise and operationalise Fundamental Duties, implementing the Justice Verma Committee’s 1999 recommendations.
                - Add new duties under Article 51-A:
                    - a. Duty to vote at elections, actively participate in democratic governance, and pay taxes.
                    - b. Duty to foster family values and responsible parenthood in education and child well-being.
                    - c. Duty of industrial organisations to provide education to employees’ children.
            5. On Parliament and State Legislatures
                - Define legislators’ privileges for independent functioning.
                - Amend Articles 105 and 194 to exclude immunity for corrupt acts and require Speaker/Chairman sanction for court cognisance of offences.
                - Maintain domiciliary requirements for Rajya Sabha elections.
                - Discontinue the MP Local Area Development Scheme.
                - Empower the Election Commission to designate “offices of profit”.
                - Establish a Nodal Standing Committee on National Economy.
                - Form a Standing Constitution Committee for constitutional amendment scrutiny.
                - Create a Legislation Committee for legislative planning.
                - Discontinue certain Parliamentary Committees (Estimates, Public Undertakings, Subordinate Legislation).
                - Introduce a parliamentary ombudsman for public scrutiny.
                - Set minimum sitting days for legislatures (50 for small states, 90 for others, 100 for Rajya Sabha, 120 for Lok Sabha).
                - Establish an external Study Group for procedural reforms.
            6. On Executive and Administration
                - In case of a hung Parliament, the Lok Sabha may elect the Leader of the House, who may then be appointed as Prime Minister by the President. The same procedure could be followed at the state level.
                - A motion of no-confidence against a Prime Minister must be accompanied by a proposal of an alternative leader to be voted simultaneously, known as the “system of constructive vote of no-confidence”.
                - For a motion of no-confidence to be brought against the government, at least 20 percent of the total number of members of the House should give notice.
                - The practice of having oversized Councils of Ministers should be prohibited by law, with a ceiling on the number of Ministers in any state or Union government fixed at a maximum of 10 percent of the total strength of the popular house of the legislature.
                - The practice of creating political offices with the position, perks, and privileges of a Minister should be discouraged, with their number limited to 2 percent of the total strength of the lower house.
                - The Constitution should provide for the appointment of a Lokpal, keeping the Prime Minister outside its purview, and the institution of Lokayuktas in the states.
                - Lateral entry into government jobs above the joint secretary level should be allowed.
                - Article 311 should be amended to ensure protection for honest public servants and penalisation for dishonest ones.
                - Questions of personnel policy, including placements, promotions, transfers, and fast-track advancements, should be managed by autonomous Civil Service Boards constituted under statutory provisions.
                - Officials, before starting their career, in addition to taking an oath of loyalty to the Constitution, should swear to abide by the principles of good governance.
                - The right to information should be guaranteed, and the traditional insistence on secrecy should be discarded, with an oath of transparency replacing an oath of secrecy.
                - Public Interest Disclosure Acts, popularly called “Whistleblower Acts”, may be enacted to fight corruption and maladministration.
                - A law should be enacted to provide for the forfeiture of benami property of corrupt public servants as well as non-public servants.
            7. On Centre-State and Inter-State Relations
                - The Inter-State Council Order of 1990 should clearly specify the matters for consultation.
                - Management of disasters and emergencies (natural and man-made) should be included in List III (Concurrent List) of the Seventh Schedule.
                - A statutory Inter-State Trade and Commerce Commission should be established.
                - The President should appoint the Governor of a state only after consultation with the Chief Minister of that state.
                - Article 356 should not be deleted but used sparingly as a last resort.
                - The question of whether a ministry in a state has lost the confidence of the assembly should be tested only on the floor of the House, and the Governor should not dismiss a ministry enjoying such confidence.
                - President’s Rule may continue without elections if elections cannot be held, with Article 356 amended accordingly.
                - The state assembly should not be dissolved before a proclamation under Article 356 is laid before Parliament, with Article 356 amended to ensure this.
                - River water disputes between states and/or the Centre should be heard by a Supreme Court bench of at least three judges, or five if necessary, for final disposal.
                - Parliament should replace the River Boards Act of 1956 with a comprehensive enactment after consultation with states.
                - When a state bill is reserved for the President’s consideration, a three-month time limit should be set for the President to decide on assent or return.
            8. On Judiciary
                - Establish a National Judicial Commission under the Constitution for Supreme Court judge appointments, comprising:
                    - a. The Chief Justice of India as chairman.
                    - b. Two senior-most Supreme Court judges.
                    - c. The Union Law Minister.
                    - d. One person nominated by the President.
                - A committee of the National Judicial Commission should examine complaints of deviant behaviour by Supreme Court and High Court judges.
                - Increase retirement ages to 65 for High Court judges and 68 for Supreme Court judges.
                - Limit contempt powers to the Supreme Court and High Courts.
                - Restrict declaration of laws as unconstitutional to the Supreme Court and High Courts.
                - Set up National and State Judicial Councils for court planning and budget proposals.
                - Judgments in the Supreme Court and High Courts should ordinarily be delivered within 90 days from case conclusion.
                - Award exemplary costs in cases of abuse of legal processes.
                - Each High Court should prepare a strategic plan for time-bound clearance of arrears, ensuring no case remains pending for more than one year.
                - Introduce plea-bargaining as part of decriminalisation.
                - Simplify the hierarchy of subordinate courts to a two-tier system under the High Court.
            9. On Pace of Socio-Economic Change and Development
                - Increase representation of SCs, STs, and Backward Classes (BCs) in higher judiciary.
                - Enable SCs, STs, and BCs, especially girls, to compete equally.
                - Create institutions to optimise resources for weaker sections.
                - Prepare Citizens’ Charters for service entitlements, especially for SCs, STs, and deprived classes.
                - Enact a statute for SC/ST/BC reservations, with Arakshan Nyaya Adalats for disputes.
                - Establish residential schools for SCs, STs, and BCs in every district.
                - Transfer Fifth Schedule tribal areas to the Sixth Schedule.
                - Set up special courts for SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act cases.
                - Enforce the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955, against untouchability.
                - Strictly implement the Employment of Manual Scavengers Act, 1993.
                - Improve minority education and political representation.
                - Establish national and state authorities for bonded labour rehabilitation.
                - Advance women’s reservations, development, empowerment, health, and protection.
            10. On Decentralisation (Panchayats and Municipalities)
                - Restructure Eleventh and Twelfth Schedules for separate fiscal domains.
                - Establish state panchayat councils under Chief Ministers.
                - Declare panchayats and municipalities as “institutions of self-government” with exclusive functions, amending Articles 243-G and 243-W.
                - Empower the Election Commission to oversee State Election Commissions, amending Articles 243-K and 243-ZA.
                - Amend Article 243-E to provide hearing opportunities before panchayat dissolution.
                - Empower the Comptroller and Auditor General to audit panchayats.
                - Require reports on municipal supersession to be tabled in state legislatures.
                - Consolidate local election qualifications in a single law.
                - Vest delimitation and reservation functions in a Delimitation Commission.
                - Recognise a distinct tax domain for municipalities.
            11. On Institutions in North East India
                - Extend 73rd and 74th Amendment opportunities to North Eastern states, respecting unique political traditions.
                - Entrust Sixth Schedule and Eleventh Schedule subjects to Autonomous District Councils.
                - Integrate traditional governance with self-governance.
                - Establish a National Immigration Council to review citizenship and migration laws.
            12. On Electoral Processes
                - Disqualify candidates charged with offences punishable by five or more years’ imprisonment.
                - Permanently bar those convicted of heinous crimes from political office.
                - Expedite criminal cases against politicians through special courts.
                - Assign election petitions to special courts or High Court election benches.
                - Defer state funding of elections until regulatory mechanisms are in place.
                - Prohibit simultaneous candidacy in multiple constituencies for the same office.
                - Give legal sanctity to the election code of conduct with penal consequences.
                - Examine a 50 percent plus one vote requirement for elections.
                - Permanently bar independent candidates losing three consecutive elections.
                - Increase the vote threshold for deposit retention to 25 percent.
                - Examine eligibility of non-Indian-born citizens for high offices through national dialogue.
                - Appoint Election Commissioners via a committee including:
                    - a. The Prime Minister.
                    - b. Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha.
                    - c. Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha.
                    - d. Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
                    - e. Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
            13. On Political Parties
                - Enact a law regulating political parties, requiring:
                    - a. Open membership irrespective of caste or community.
                    - b. Systematic financial accounts.
                    - c. Candidate asset declarations at nomination.
                    - d. No tickets for candidates convicted or charged with criminal offences.
                    - e. Disqualification and deregistration for violations.
                - Increase recognition thresholds to limit party proliferation.
                - Enact a law for transparent political funding, including:
                    - a. Transparency in political funding.
                    - b. Higher prescribed limits for corporate donations.
                    - c. Tax exemptions for donations up to a specified limit.
                    - d. Accountability for donors and donees.
                    - e. Annual publication of audited party accounts.
                    - f. Penalties for false election returns.
            14. On Anti-Defection Law
                - Amend the Tenth Schedule to provide:
                    - a. All defectors must resign and recontest elections.
                    - b. Defectors are barred from public office for the remaining term or until next elections.
                    - c. Votes by defectors to topple governments are invalid.
                    - d. Disqualification decisions vest in the Election Commission, not the Speaker/Chairman.


- Chapter 90: Landmark Judgements and Their Impact
    - Romesh Thappar Case (1950)
        - Name of the Case: Romesh Thappar vs. State of Madras
        - Year of Judgement: 1950
        - Popular Name: Cross Roads case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Freedom of the press
        - Related Article/Schedule: 19
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - The freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) includes freedom of propagation of ideas, ensured by the freedom of circulation. Without liberty of circulation, publication would be of little value.
            - The order of the Madras government banning the entry and circulation of the weekly English journal Cross Roads, published in Bombay, was declared unconstitutional and void. The ban was issued under Section 9(1-A) of the Madras Maintenance of Public Order Act, 1949.
            - Freedom of speech and the press are foundational to democratic organisations, as free political discussion is essential for public education and the proper functioning of popular government.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - The 1st Amendment Act (1951) added “public order” as a reasonable restriction under Article 19(2) on freedom of speech and expression.
            - The Supreme Court held that restrictions could only be imposed on grounds mentioned in Article 19(2). It refused to permit restrictions on the ground of public order, as it was not listed in Article 19(2) at the time.
            - Ordinary or local breaches of public order were not grounds for restricting freedom of speech and expression.
            - The term “public order” has a wide connotation, signifying a state of tranquillity among members of political society due to internal regulations enforced by the government.

    - A.K. Gopalan Case (1950)
        - Name of the Case: A.K. Gopalan vs. State of Madras
        - Year of Judgement: 1950
        - Popular Name: Preventive Detention case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Procedure established by law
        - Related Article/Schedule: 21 & 22
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Section 14 of the Preventive Detention Act (1950) was invalidated for violating the fundamental right under Article 22. Its omission did not alter the Act’s nature, structure, or object, so the rest of the Act remained valid.
            - The expression “personal liberty” under Article 21 means liberty of the physical body, i.e., freedom from physical restraint or detention.
            - Article 21 protects against executive action but not against the legislature.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - The Supreme Court adopted a narrow, textualist interpretation of Article 21, viewing “law” as state-made law, not principles of natural justice.
            - The expression “procedure established by law” in Article 21 was distinguished from the American “due process of law”.
            - Protection under Article 21 was limited to arbitrary executive action, not legislative action.
            - This interpretation held for nearly three decades (1950–1978), reaching its logical end in the A.D.M. Jabalpur case (1976). It was overruled in the Maneka Gandhi case (1978) with a wider interpretation of Article 21.

    - Champakam Dorairajan Case (1951)
        - Name of the Case: State of Madras vs. Champakam Dorairajan
        - Year of Judgement: 1951
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Communal reservation in admission to educational institutions
        - Related Article/Schedule: 15, 29 & 46
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Affirmed the Madras High Court’s judgement, striking down the Madras government’s Communal GO, which provided proportionate reservation in medical and engineering colleges to promote backward classes under Article 46.
            - The Communal GO was based on religion, race, and caste, violating Articles 15(1) and 29(2).
            - Directive Principles cannot override or abridge Fundamental Rights and must conform to and run subsidiary to them.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Led to the insertion of Clause (4) in Article 15 by the 1st Amendment Act (1951), permitting special provisions for the advancement of socially and educationally backward classes, Scheduled Castes (SCs), and Scheduled Tribes (STs).
            - Nullified the effect of the judgement.

    - Shankari Prasad Case (1951)
        - Name of the Case: Shankari Prasad vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 1951
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution
        - Related Article/Schedule: 13 & 368
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Parliament’s amending power under Article 368 includes the power to amend Fundamental Rights in Part III.
            - A constitutional amendment act abridging or taking away Fundamental Rights is not void under Article 13(2).
            - Upheld the validity of the 1st Amendment Act (1951), which curtailed the right to property by inserting Articles 31A and 31B.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Distinguished between ordinary legislative law and constituent law (constitutional amendment law).
            - The word “law” in Article 13(2) refers to ordinary law, not constituent law under Article 368.
            - Parliament can amend any constitutional provision, rejecting the view that Fundamental Rights are inviolable.
            - This judgement held for one and a half decades (1951–1967), reaffirmed in the Sajjan Singh case (1964), but overruled in the I.C. Golak Nath case (1967).

    - Berubari Union Case (1960)
        - Name of the Case: Berubari Union vs. Unknown
        - Year of Judgement: 1960
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: -
        - Related Article/Schedule: -
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Parliament’s power under Article 3 to diminish a state’s area does not cover cession of Indian territory to a foreign country, as Article 3 deals with internal adjustments among constituent states.
            - Cession of Indian territory requires a constitutional amendment under Article 368, altering the First Schedule.
            - The Preamble is not part of the Constitution.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Led to the 9th Amendment Act (1960), giving effect to the transfer of Berubari Union (West Bengal) to Pakistan under the Indo-Pak (Nehru-Noon) Agreement of 1958.

    - K.M. Nanavati Case (1961)
        - Name of the Case: K.M. Nanavati vs. State of Maharashtra
        - Year of Judgement: 1961
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Jury system of trial
        - Related Article/Schedule: -
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Affirmed the Bombay High Court’s judgement, upholding the conviction of Nanavati under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code and the life imprisonment sentence for the murder of his wife’s paramour.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Highlighted shortcomings in the jury system, leading to its abolition.
            - Some jury trials continued post-judgement, but the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, completely removed the jury trial system.
            - Nanavati, after three years in prison, was granted pardon by the Governor.

    - I.C. Golak Nath Case (1967)
        - Name of the Case: I.C. Golak Nath vs. State of Punjab
        - Year of Judgement: 1967
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution
        - Related Article/Schedule: 13 & 368
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Overruled Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1964), holding that the amending power under Article 368 cannot abridge or take away Fundamental Rights in Part III.
            - A constitutional amendment act is a “law” under Article 13(2).
            - Applied prospective overruling, allowing the 1st (1951), 4th (1955), and 17th (1964) Amendment Acts to remain valid for the future.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Led to the 24th Amendment Act (1971), which clarified Parliament’s power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, and excluded constitutional amendments from Article 13(2).

    - Kesavananda Bharati Case (1973)
        - Name of the Case: Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala
        - Year of Judgement: 1973
        - Popular Name: Fundamental Rights case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Parliament’s power to amend the Constitution
        - Related Article/Schedule: 13 & 368
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Overruled I.C. Golak Nath (1967), holding that Parliament can amend any constitutional provision, including Fundamental Rights, under Article 368, except the “basic structure” of the Constitution.
            - Upheld the 24th Amendment Act (1971), which inserted Clause (4) in Article 13 and Clause (3) in Article 368.
            - Validated Sections 2(a) and 2(b) of the 25th Amendment Act (1971) but declared the first part of Section 3 valid and the second part invalid. The second part stated: “No law containing a declaration that it is for giving effect to such policy shall be called in question in any court on the ground that it does not give effect to such policy.”
            - Validated the 29th Amendment Act (1971).
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Established the doctrine of basic structure as a limitation on Parliament’s amending power.
            - The doctrine was applied in subsequent cases to assess amendment validity and expanded the list of basic structure elements.
            - Led to the 42nd Amendment Act (1976), granting Parliament unlimited amending power, addressed in the next case.

    - Indira Nehru Gandhi Case (1975)
        - Name of the Case: Indira Nehru Gandhi vs. Raj Narain
        - Year of Judgement: 1975
        - Popular Name: Election case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Basic structure of the Constitution
        - Related Article/Schedule: 329A (Repealed)
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Reaffirmed the basic structure doctrine, striking down Clause (4) of Article 329A, inserted by the 39th Amendment Act (1975), which excluded election disputes involving the Prime Minister and Lok Sabha Speaker from court jurisdiction.
            - Held that this provision violated the basic structure.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Following Kesavananda Bharati and this case, the 42nd Amendment Act (1976) inserted Clauses (4) and (5) in Article 368, prohibiting judicial review of amendments and removing limitations on Parliament’s amending power.
            - Article 329A was repealed by the 44th Amendment Act (1978).

    - A.D.M. Jabalpur Case (1976)
        - Name of the Case: A.D.M. Jabalpur vs. Shivakant Shukla
        - Year of Judgement: 1976
        - Popular Name: Habeas Corpus case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Right to life and personal liberty during emergency
        - Related Article/Schedule: 21 & 359
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Article 21 is the sole repository of the right to life and personal liberty against the state.
            - If Article 21 is suspended by a Presidential Order under Article 359, a detenu has no locus standi to file a writ petition challenging detention legality.
            - Upheld the constitutional validity of Section 16A(9) of the Maintenance of Internal Security Act (MISA), 1971.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Took a restrictive view of Article 21, failing to protect Fundamental Rights during the 1975–77 emergency.
            - The 44th Amendment Act (1978) amended Article 359 to prevent suspension of Article 21, rendering this judgement of academic importance only.

    - Maneka Gandhi Case (1978)
        - Name of the Case: Maneka Gandhi vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 1978
        - Popular Name: Personal Liberty case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Procedure established by law
        - Related Article/Schedule: 21
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Overruled A.K. Gopalan (1950), declaring Section 10(3)(c) of the Passport Act (1967) valid, not violative of Articles 14, 19(1)(a), or (g), and 21.
            - Laid down propositions:
                - a. Articles 14, 19, and 21 are not mutually exclusive; a law depriving personal liberty must pass tests under all three articles.
                - b. “Personal liberty” in Article 21 is wide, covering various rights, some elevated to distinct Fundamental Rights under Article 19.
                - c. The right to life under Article 21 includes aspects making life meaningful, complete, and worth living, including human dignity.
                - d. “Procedure established by law” in Article 21 means just, fair, and reasonable procedure, conforming to natural justice principles, not arbitrary or oppressive.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Introduced the American “due process of law” concept in Indian judicial interpretation.
            - Established the “golden triangle” rule (interrelation of Articles 14, 19, and 21).
            - Expanded Article 21’s scope, enabling subsequent cases to declare various rights as integral to Article 21.

    - Bachan Singh Case (1980)
        - Name of the Case: Bachan Singh vs. State of Punjab
        - Year of Judgement: 1980
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Constitutional validity of death penalty
        - Related Article/Schedule: 19 & 21
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - The death penalty under Section 302 of the Indian Penal Code, as an alternative punishment for murder, is not unreasonable and does not violate Article 19’s letter or ethos.
            - Article 19(1) does not guarantee the activity of committing murder.
            - The death penalty does not violate Article 21, which recognises the state’s right to deprive life or liberty per fair, just, and reasonable procedure.
            - Death penalty should be an exception, confined to “rarest of rare cases” when no alternative exists, considering the crime’s and criminal’s exceptional and grave circumstances.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Established the “rarest of rare cases” doctrine for awarding death penalties, influencing subsequent Supreme Court judgements.

    - Minerva Mills Case (1980)
        - Name of the Case: Minerva Mills vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 1980
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Basic structure of the Constitution
        - Related Article/Schedule: 31C & 368
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Invalidated Clauses (4) and (5) of Article 368 and the amendment to Article 31C, inserted by the 42nd Amendment Act (1976), for destroying the Constitution’s basic structure.
            - Identified limited parliamentary amending power, judicial review, and harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles as basic features.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Nullified the 42nd Amendment’s attempt to grant Parliament unlimited amending power and prioritise all Directive Principles over Fundamental Rights under Articles 14, 19, and 31 (Article 31 was later omitted by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978).
            - Held that destroying the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles destroys the Constitution’s basic structure.

    - Waman Rao Case (1980)
        - Name of the Case: Waman Rao vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 1980
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Judicial review of the Ninth Schedule
        - Related Article/Schedule: 368 & Ninth Schedule
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Amendments to the Ninth Schedule before 24 April 1973 (Kesavananda Bharati judgement date) are valid.
            - Amendments after 24 April 1973 are open to challenge if they damage the Constitution’s basic structure.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Established that post-1973 Ninth Schedule amendments are subject to judicial review for basic structure violations.

    - Shah Bano Case (1985)
        - Name of the Case: Mohd. Ahmed Khan vs. Shah Bano
        - Year of Judgement: 1985
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Maintenance of a divorced Muslim wife
        - Related Article/Schedule: -
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Upheld the Madhya Pradesh High Court’s judgement, ruling that a Muslim husband is liable to pay maintenance to a divorced wife beyond the iddat period.
            - Section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, is secular, applies to all religions, and prevails over personal law in conflicts.
            - Mahr (dower) does not absolve a Muslim husband from maintenance obligations.
            - Emphasised that a uniform civil code would promote national integration by reducing conflicting legal loyalties.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Led to the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986, which limited maintenance to the iddat period, overturning the judgement.
            - In Danial Latifi case (2001), the Supreme Court upheld the 1986 Act’s validity but ruled that maintenance extends beyond iddat.

    - D.C. Wadhwa Case (1986)
        - Name of the Case: D.C. Wadhwa vs. State of Bihar
        - Year of Judgement: 1986
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Ordinance-making power of the Governor
        - Related Article/Schedule: 213
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Noted that between 1967–1981, the Bihar Governor promulgated 256 ordinances, kept in force for 1–14 years via re-promulgation.
            - Held that the exceptional power under Article 213 cannot substitute for the state legislature’s law-making power.
            - Declared such re-promulgation a “subversion of the democratic process” and a “fraud on the Constitution”.
            - Declared the re-promulgated Bihar Intermediate Education Council Ordinance, 1985, unconstitutional and invalid.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Exposed misuse of the Governor’s ordinance-making power by the executive.

    - M.C. Mehta Case (1986)
        - Name of the Case: M.C. Mehta vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 1986
        - Popular Name: Oleum Gas Leak case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Power of the Supreme Court to award compensation
        - Related Article/Schedule: 21 & 32
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - The power under Article 32 is not only injunctive (preventing Fundamental Rights infringement) but also remedial, including compensation in appropriate cases.
            - Compensation applies to gross, patent, incontrovertible, and ex facie glaring Fundamental Rights infringements.
            - Applications for compensation to enforce the right to life under Article 21 are maintainable under Article 32.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Expanded environmental law by introducing the principle of absolute liability (no-fault liability), replacing strict liability.

    - Kihoto Hollohan Case (1992)
        - Name of the Case: Kihoto Hollohan vs. Zachillhu
        - Year of Judgement: 1992
        - Popular Name: Defection case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Validity of anti-defection law
        - Related Article/Schedule: 368 & Tenth Schedule
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Declared paragraph 7 of the Tenth Schedule, inserted by the 52nd Amendment Act (1985), unconstitutional for violating Article 368(2) by not being ratified by half the state legislatures.
            - Paragraph 7 excluded Supreme Court (Article 136) and High Court (Article 226) jurisdiction.
            - Upheld the validity of the remaining Tenth Schedule provisions.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Clarified the need for state legislature ratification for amendments affecting judicial jurisdiction.

    - Indra Sawhney Case (1992)
        - Name of the Case: Indra Sawhney vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 1992
        - Popular Name: Mandal case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Reservation for OBCs in government jobs
        - Related Article/Schedule: 16
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Upheld the executive order providing 27% reservation for Other Backward Classes (OBCs) under Article 16(4), with conditions:
                - a. Exclusion of the creamy layer.
                - b. No reservation in promotions.
                - c. Maximum reservation not to exceed 50%.
                - d. 50% ceiling on backlog vacancies.
                - e. No relaxation in qualifying marks for promotions.
            - Invalidated a 10% reservation order for other economically backward sections not covered by existing schemes.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Led to:
                - a. Appointment of the Ram Nandan Committee to identify the creamy layer among OBCs.
                - b. Establishment of the statutory National Commission for Backward Classes (later granted constitutional status by the 102nd Amendment Act, 2018, inserting Article 338-B).
                - c. Enactment of five amendment acts:
                    - (i). 76th Amendment Act (1994), placing Tamil Nadu’s reservation act in the Ninth Schedule.
                    - (ii). 77th Amendment Act (1995), nullifying the no-reservation-in-promotions ruling.
                    - (iii). 81st Amendment Act (2000), nullifying the backlog vacancies ruling.
                    - (iv). 82nd Amendment Act (2000), allowing relaxations in qualifying marks for promotions.
                    - (v). 85th Amendment Act (2001), providing consequential seniority in promotions for SCs/STs.

    - Mohini Jain Case (1992)
        - Name of the Case: Mohini Jain vs. State of Karnataka
        - Year of Judgement: 1992
        - Popular Name: Capitation Fee case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Right to education
        - Related Article/Schedule: 21 & 41
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Declared the right to education a Fundamental Right under Article 21, extending to professional education (e.g., engineering, medicine).
            - The right to life and individual dignity under Article 21 requires the right to education.
            - Without realising the Directive Principle under Article 41, Fundamental Rights remain inaccessible to the illiterate majority.
            - Charging capitation fees for admission violates Article 14 by denying the right to education arbitrarily.
            - Capitation fees are a “price for selling education”, contrary to the constitutional scheme.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Formed the basis for the Unni Krishnan case (1993), which led to the 86th Amendment Act (2002).
            - The Unni Krishnan case partly upheld and partly overruled this judgement.

    - Unni Krishnan Case (1993)
        - Name of the Case: Unni Krishnan vs. State of Andhra Pradesh
        - Year of Judgement: 1993
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Right to education
        - Related Article/Schedule: 21 & 45
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - The right to education is a Fundamental Right under Article 21, flowing from the right to life.
            - Children have a right to free education until age 14; post-14, state obligation depends on economic capacity.
            - The state must follow Article 45 (pre-2002 amendment), providing free and compulsory education up to age 14.
            - Article 21 is to be read with Directive Principles (Articles 41, 45, 46).
            - The state can discharge obligations by establishing institutions or aiding private ones.
            - Private unaided professional institutions can charge higher fees than government institutions, within a ceiling, without commercialising education.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Led to the 86th Amendment Act (2002), inserting Article 21A, making free and compulsory education for ages 6–14 a Fundamental Right.
            - The Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education (RTE) Act, 2009, gave effect to Article 21A.
