    - Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association Case (1993)
        - Name of the Case: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 1993
        - Popular Name: Second Judges case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Appointment of Supreme Court and High Court Judges
        - Related Article/Schedule: 124 & 217
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Overruled S.P. Gupta (1981) (First Judges case), holding that Supreme Court and High Court judges are appointed by the President per the Chief Justice of India’s (CJI) advice, after consulting two senior-most colleagues.
            - Changed “consultation” in Articles 124(2) and 217(1) to “concurrence”.
            - The senior-most Supreme Court judge should be appointed CJI.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Established the collegium system for judicial appointments, formalised via a Memorandum of Procedure following this case and the Third Judges case (1998).

    - S.R. Bommai Case (1994)
        - Name of the Case: S.R. Bommai vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 1994
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: President’s Rule
        - Related Article/Schedule: 356
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Upheld President’s Rule under Article 356 in Madhya Pradesh, Himachal Pradesh, and Rajasthan (1992) but declared it unconstitutional in Nagaland (1988), Karnataka (1989), and Meghalaya (1991).
            - Laid down propositions:
                - a. The validity of a proclamation under Article 356(1) is subject to judicial review.
                - b. The Union Government must prove the existence of relevant material justifying the proclamation.
                - c. Article 74(2) does not bar scrutiny of the material basis for the President’s satisfaction.
                - d. If a proclamation is invalid, courts can restore the Legislative Assembly and Ministry, despite parliamentary approval.
                - e. Secularism is part of the basic structure; a state government’s anti-secular acts justify President’s Rule.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Checked arbitrary use of Article 356 by the Centre for imposing President’s Rule.

    - Vishaka Case (1997)
        - Name of the Case: Vishaka vs. State of Rajasthan
        - Year of Judgement: 1997
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Sexual harassment of women at workplace
        - Related Article/Schedule: 15 & 21
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Sexual harassment at the workplace violates Articles 15 and 21.
            - Employers or responsible persons in public or private workplaces must prevent sexual harassment.
            - Issued detailed guidelines (Vishaka Guidelines) to be followed until legislation is enacted.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Filled a legislative vacuum, as no domestic law addressed workplace sexual harassment beyond Indian Penal Code provisions.
            - Led to the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.

    - Vineet Narain Case (1997)
        - Name of the Case: Vineet Narain vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 1997
        - Popular Name: Jain Hawala case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Autonomy and efficient functioning of CBI
        - Related Article/Schedule: -
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Directed statutory status for the Central Vigilance Commission (CVC).
            - Issued directions to make the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) and Enforcement Directorate (ED) autonomous and non-partisan.
            - Struck down the Single Directive, requiring CBI to obtain Central Government permission before investigating officers of Joint Secretary rank and above.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Led to the CVC Act, 2003, granting statutory status to the CVC and vesting CBI superintendence in corruption cases with the CVC.
            - The Single Directive was reinstated by the CVC Act but declared invalid again in 2014 for violating Article 14.

    - Association for Democratic Reforms Case (2002)
        - Name of the Case: Union of India vs. Association for Democratic Reforms
        - Year of Judgement: 2002
        - Popular Name: Poll Reforms case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Criminalisation of politics
        - Related Article/Schedule: 19
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - A voter’s right to know a candidate’s antecedents, including criminal past, is part of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).
            - Voting is an expression; democracy requires free, informed voters.
            - Directed the Election Commission to mandate candidates to furnish:
                - a. Details of past convictions/acquittals/discharges, including punishments.
                - b. Pending cases within six months of nomination, with offences punishable by two or more years’ imprisonment, including court details.
                - c. Assets of the candidate, spouse, and dependents.
                - d. Liabilities, including dues to public financial institutions or government.
                - e. Educational qualifications.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - The Election Commission’s 2003 order (27 March 2003) mandated candidates to provide the above information on nomination papers.
            - Furnishing false information became an electoral offence.

    - T.M.A. Pai Foundation Case (2002)
        - Name of the Case: T.M.A. Pai Foundation vs. State of Karnataka
        - Year of Judgement: 2002
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Rights of minority educational institutions
        - Related Article/Schedule: 29 & 30
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Laid down propositions for minority educational institutions (aided and unaided):
                - a. Linguistic and religious minorities are covered under Article 30; minority status is determined state-wise due to linguistic state reorganisation.
                - b. Article 30(1) grants minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions of their choice, including professional institutions.
                - c. State or university cannot regulate admissions to unaided minority institutions, except for setting qualifications and minimum eligibility for academic standards.
                - d. The right to administer is not absolute; regulatory measures can ensure educational standards and excellence.
                - e. Aided minority institutions are governed by Article 29(2), prohibiting admission refusals based on religion, race, caste, or language.
                - f. Aided professional institutions may require passing a state-conducted common entrance test.
                - g. Minority institutions may have fair, transparent admission procedures, with merit-based selection for professional and higher education.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - The 93rd Amendment Act (2005) inserted Clause (5) in Article 15, empowering the state to make special provisions for backward classes, SCs, and STs in admissions to private institutions (except minority institutions under Article 30(1)), overcoming this and the Inamdar case (2005).

    - Naveen Jindal Case (2004)
        - Name of the Case: Union of India vs. Naveen Jindal
        - Year of Judgement: 2004
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Right to fly the national flag
        - Related Article/Schedule: 19
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - The right to fly the national flag freely with respect and dignity is a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(a), expressing allegiance and national pride.
            - The flag cannot be used for commercial purposes or otherwise.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Affirmed citizens’ right to display the national flag, subject to respect and dignity.

    - Prakash Singh Case (2006)
        - Name of the Case: Prakash Singh vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2006
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Police reforms
        - Related Article/Schedule: -
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Issued seven directives to ensure police function without political interference:
                - (i). Constitute a State Security Commission.
                - (ii). Select the Director General of Police (DGP) from the three senior-most officers empanelled by UPSC, with a minimum two-year tenure.
                - (iii). Ensure a two-year tenure for police officers on operational duties.
                - (iv). Separate investigation police from law and order police.
                - (v). Set up a Police Establishment Board.
                - (vi). Establish Police Complaints Authorities at state and district levels.
                - (vii). Form a National Security Commission at the central level.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Partially introduced police reforms, but political interference in postings/transfers persists.
            - State Security Commissions and Police Establishment Boards exist in most states but lack effective authority.
            - High Courts have issued compliance orders in various cases.

    - M. Nagaraj Case (2006)
        - Name of the Case: M. Nagaraj vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2006
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Reservation in promotions for SCs and STs
        - Related Article/Schedule: 16 & 335
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Upheld the constitutional validity of the 77th (1995), 81st (2000), 82nd (2000), and 85th (2001) Amendment Acts, inserting Articles 16(4A) and 16(4B).
            - These amendments flow from Article 16(4), retaining backwardness, inadequate representation, and overall administrative efficiency (Article 335) as controlling factors.
            - Amendments apply only to SCs/STs, preserving constitutional requirements like the 50% ceiling, creamy layer exclusion, sub-classification, and post-based rosters.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Affirmed the constitutional framework for SC/ST reservations in promotions.

    - I.R. Coelho Case (2007)
        - Name of the Case: I.R. Coelho vs. State of Tamil Nadu
        - Year of Judgement: 2007
        - Popular Name: Ninth Schedule case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Judicial review of the Ninth Schedule
        - Related Article/Schedule: 31B & Ninth Schedule
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Reaffirmed Waman Rao (1980), holding that post-24 April 1973 Ninth Schedule amendments are challengeable if they damage the basic structure.
            - Established tests to assess the validity of such amendments.
            - Questioned whether Parliament can immunise legislation from Fundamental Rights under Article 31B by adding it to the Ninth Schedule post-1973.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Reinforced judicial review of Ninth Schedule amendments for basic structure compliance.

    - Aruna Ramachandra Shanbaug Case (2011)
        - Name of the Case: Aruna Ramachandra Shanbaug vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2011
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Euthanasia
        - Related Article/Schedule: 21
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Active euthanasia and assisted death are illegal; passive euthanasia is permissible with conditions:
                - (i). Life support discontinuation decisions can be made by parents, spouse, close relatives, a next friend, or doctors.
                - (ii). Such decisions require High Court approval.
                - (iii). The High Court Chief Justice must constitute a two-judge bench, seeking a three-doctor committee’s opinion.
                - (iv). The bench must issue notice to the state, close relatives, or next friend and provide the doctor committee’s report, giving a verdict after hearing them.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Established a framework for passive euthanasia with judicial oversight.

    - People’s Union for Civil Liberties Case (2013)
        - Name of the Case: People’s Union for Civil Liberties vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2013
        - Popular Name: NOTA case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Electoral reforms
        - Related Article/Schedule: 14, 19 & 21
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Declared Rules 41(2), (3), and 49-O of the Conduct of Election Rules, 1961, ultra vires Section 128 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, and Article 19(1)(a) for violating voting secrecy.
            - Directed the Election Commission to provide a “None of the Above” (NOTA) button on EVMs for voters opting not to vote while maintaining secrecy.
            - Observations:
                - (i). The right not to vote under Section 79(d) and Rule 49-O requires secrecy protection akin to voters who cast votes.
                - (ii). NOTA ensures the right of expression under Article 19(1)(a) and avoids discrimination (Article 14).
                - (iii). Article 19 guarantees speech, criticism, and disagreement; denying negative voting defeats freedom of expression and liberty (Article 21).
                - (iv). Secrecy is integral to free and fair elections; distinguishing between voters who cast and abstain violates Article 14.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - The Election Commission introduced NOTA in EVMs starting with 2013 state elections (Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Mizoram, Delhi, Rajasthan) and continued in 2014 elections.

    - Lily Thomas Case (2013)
        - Name of the Case: Lily Thomas vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2013
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Criminalisation of politics
        - Related Article/Schedule: 102 & 191
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Convicted MPs and state legislators lose membership immediately upon conviction.
            - Struck down Section 8(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951, which allowed a three-month appeal period, as unconstitutional.
            - Parliament lacks power under Articles 102 and 191 to differentiate disqualification rules for candidates and sitting members.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Led to immediate disqualification of convicted legislators.
            - The Representation of the People (Second Amendment and Validation) Bill, 2013, to nullify the ruling was introduced but later withdrawn.

    - T.S.R. Subramanian Case (2013)
        - Name of the Case: T.S.R. Subramanian vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2013
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Civil service reforms
        - Related Article/Schedule: -
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Issued directives for civil service reforms:
                - (i). Constitute Civil Service Boards to advise on transfers, postings, disciplinary actions, and service matters.
                - (ii). Provide fixed minimum tenure for civil servants.
                - (iii). Mandate written and recorded instructions, prohibiting action on verbal orders.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Led to amendments in Rule 7 of IAS, IPS, and IFoS (Cadre) Rules (2014).
            - Central Services’ Cadre Controlling Authorities were directed to implement the reforms.
            - Civil Service Boards in states/UTs remain ineffective.

    - National Legal Services Authority Case (2014)
        - Name of the Case: National Legal Services Authority vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2014
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Rights of transgender persons
        - Related Article/Schedule: 14 & 21
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Declared transgenders, including hijras/eunuchs, as a “third gender” with equal Fundamental Rights under Part III.
            - Upheld transgender persons’ right to self-identify their gender (male, female, or third gender).
            - Directed governments to grant legal gender recognition and treat transgenders as socially and educationally backward classes, extending reservations in education and public appointments.
            - Non-recognition of transgender identity denies equal protection under Article 14.
            - Gender identity is integral to dignity, personal autonomy, and self-determination under Article 21.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Led to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, prohibiting discrimination and recognising self-perceived gender identity.

    - Shreya Singhal Case (2015)
        - Name of the Case: Shreya Singhal vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2015
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Restrictions on online speech
        - Related Article/Schedule: 19
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Struck down Section 66A of the Information Technology Act (2000) for violating Article 19(1)(a) as vague and overbroad.
            - The section, punishing offensive messages via computer or communication devices, was not saved by Article 19(2).
            - Internet’s wider circulation does not justify restricting Article 19(1)(a) rights.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Protected online free speech by removing vague legal restrictions.

    - Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association Case (2015)
        - Name of the Case: Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2015
        - Popular Name: Fourth Judges case or NJAC case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Appointment of Supreme Court and High Court Judges
        - Related Article/Schedule: 124 & 217
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Declared the 99th Amendment Act (2014) and National Judicial Appointments Commission (NJAC) Act (2014) unconstitutional for affecting judicial independence, a basic structure component.
            - Restored the collegium system for judicial appointments.
            - Ordered further consideration of measures to improve the collegium system.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Invalidated the NJAC, reinstating the collegium system.

    - Shayara Bano Case (2017)
        - Name of the Case: Shayara Bano vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2017
        - Popular Name: Triple Talaq case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Divorce in the Muslim community
        - Related Article/Schedule: 14
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Declared triple talaq (talaq-e-biddat) unconstitutional for being manifestly arbitrary, allowing capricious divorce without reconciliation, violating Article 14.
            - Declared Section 2 of the Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937, void to the extent it recognises triple talaq.
            - Held that triple talaq contradicts the Quran’s tenets and is bad in law.
            - Directed the Centre to legislate on Muslim divorce within six months, with an injunction against triple talaq until then.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Led to the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019 (Triple Talaq Act), prohibiting talaq pronouncement and protecting married Muslim women’s rights.

    - K.S. Puttaswamy Case (2017)
        - Name of the Case: K.S. Puttaswamy vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2017
        - Popular Name: Right to Privacy case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Fundamental right to privacy
        - Related Article/Schedule: 21
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Declared the right to privacy a Fundamental Right under Article 21 and Part III freedoms, safeguarding individual autonomy and control over vital life aspects.
            - Privacy is not absolute and is subject to reasonable restrictions under Part III.
            - Laws encroaching on privacy must be fair, just, and reasonable, meeting:
                - (i). Legality (existence of law).
                - (ii). Need (legitimate state aim).
                - (iii). Proportionality (rational nexus between objects and means).
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962), which denied privacy as a constitutional right.
            - Affirmed subsequent judgements recognising privacy.
            - Influenced cases like Indian Young Lawyers Association (2018), Joseph Shine (2018), and Navtej Singh Johar (2018).
            - In a separate 2018 judgement (Puttaswamy-II or Aadhaar case), upheld the Aadhaar Act, 2016, ruling it does not violate privacy, with struck-down provisions and amendments via the Aadhaar and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2019.

    - Indian Young Lawyers Association Case (2018)
        - Name of the Case: Indian Young Lawyers Association vs. State of Kerala
        - Year of Judgement: 2018
        - Popular Name: Sabarimala case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Women’s entry into Sabarimala temple
        - Related Article/Schedule: 14, 21 & 25
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Allowed women of all ages to enter and worship at Sabarimala temple.
            - Declared the ban on women aged 10–50 unconstitutional, violating Articles 14, 21, and 25.
            - Struck down Rule 3(h) of the Kerala Hindu Places of Public Worship (Authorisation of Entry) Rules, 1965.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Sparked protests and hartals by devotees in Kerala; some women faced resistance but others entered successfully.
            - In November 2019, a five-judge review bench referred the case to a larger bench; a nine-judge bench was constituted for adjudication.

    - Joseph Shine Case (2018)
        - Name of the Case: Joseph Shine vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2018
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Decriminalisation of adultery
        - Related Article/Schedule: 14, 15 & 21
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Decriminalised adultery, striking down Section 497 of the Indian Penal Code and Section 198(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (as applicable to adultery) as unconstitutional for violating Articles 14, 15, and 21.
            - When the substantive provision is struck, the procedural provision follows.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Overruled prior judgements upholding Section 497.
            - Adultery is no longer a criminal offence but remains a civil wrong and ground for divorce.

    - Navtej Singh Johar Case (2018)
        - Name of the Case: Navtej Singh Johar vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2018
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Decriminalisation of homosexuality
        - Related Article/Schedule: 14, 15, 19 & 21
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Decriminalised homosexuality, partly striking down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code for criminalising consensual same-sex adult acts.
            - Declared such criminalisation unconstitutional, violating Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(a), and 21.
            - LGBT persons are entitled to equal Fundamental Rights.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Overruled Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013), which upheld Section 377’s validity.
            - Allowed consensual same-sex conduct, while Section 377 governs non-consensual acts, minors, and bestiality.

    - M. Siddiq Case (2019)
        - Name of the Case: M. Siddiq vs. Mahant Suresh Das
        - Year of Judgement: 2019
        - Popular Name: Ayodhya case
        - Related Topic/Issue: Babri Masjid land dispute
        - Related Article/Schedule: -
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Awarded the 2.77-acre disputed land in Ayodhya to deity Ram Lalla Virajman.
            - Directed:
                - (i). The Centre to formulate a scheme for a trust to construct a Ram Mandir at the site.
                - (ii). The Centre and Uttar Pradesh government to allot 5 acres of alternative land to the UP Sunni Central Waqf Board in Ayodhya for a mosque.
                - (iii). The scheme to include appropriate representation for Nirmohi Akhara.
            - Dismissed Nirmohi Akhara’s suit claiming shebaiti rights as barred by limitation.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Resolved a century-old dispute affecting communal harmony.
            - The Centre formed the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra trust.
            - Uttar Pradesh allocated 5 acres in Dhannipur, Ayodhya, to the Waqf Board.
            - Overturned the 2010 Allahabad High Court’s equal division of the land among three parties.

    - Anuradha Bhasin Case (2020)
        - Name of the Case: Anuradha Bhasin vs. Union of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2020
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Suspension of internet services
        - Related Article/Schedule: 19
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Held:
                - (i). Freedom of speech and expression and freedom to practice any profession or trade via the internet are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g), subject to restrictions under Articles 19(2) and (6), including proportionality.
                - (ii). Indefinite internet suspension is impermissible under the Temporary Suspension of Telecom Services (Public Emergency or Public Safety) Rules, 2017; suspensions must be temporary.
                - (iii). Internet suspension orders must adhere to proportionality and not extend beyond necessary duration.
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Established the right to internet access as a Fundamental Right under the Constitution.
            - Recognised the government’s right to suspend internet services with proportionality, potentially causing conflicts.

    - Rambabu Singh Thakur Case (2020)
        - Name of the Case: Rambabu Singh Thakur vs. Sunil Arora
        - Year of Judgement: 2020
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Criminalisation of politics
        - Related Article/Schedule: -
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Issued directives to curb criminalisation in politics:
                - (i). Political parties must upload detailed information on candidates with pending criminal cases, including offence nature, court, and case number, and reasons for selection over candidates without criminal antecedents.
                - (ii). Selection reasons must focus on qualifications, achievements, and merit, not mere winnability.
                - (iii). Information must be published in one local vernacular newspaper, one national newspaper, and the party’s official social media platforms (e.g., Facebook, Twitter).
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - The Election Commission directed parties to comply, introducing Form C-7 for reporting candidates with criminal backgrounds.
            
    - Internet and Mobile Association of India Case (2020)
        - Name of the Case: Internet and Mobile Association of India vs. Reserve Bank of India
        - Year of Judgement: 2020
        - Popular Name: -
        - Related Topic/Issue: Ban on cryptocurrency trading
        - Related Article/Schedule: 19
        - Supreme Court Judgement:
            - Struck down an RBI circular directing banks and financial institutions not to deal in virtual currencies (VCs) or provide VC-related services, declaring it illegal and unenforceable for lacking proportionality.
            - The RBI found no loss or adverse effect on banks from VC exchanges.
            - The circular violated freedom to trade under Article 19(1)(g).
        - Impact of the Judgement:
            - Lifted the ban on cryptocurrency trading, allowing banks to rejoin the VC industry.
            - Highlighted the need for a legal framework to regulate cryptocurrency trading in India.

- Chapter 91: Important Doctrines of Constitutional Interpretation
    - Doctrine of Severability
        - 1. Meaning of the Doctrine
            - The doctrine of severability, also known as the doctrine of separability, was developed by the Supreme Court to address the validity of laws declared unconstitutional.
            - When a law is partially unconstitutional, the question arises whether the entire law is void or only the unconstitutional part. According to this doctrine, if the unconstitutional provision can be separated from the constitutional provisions, only the offending part is declared void, not the entire law.
            - If the valid and invalid parts cannot be separated, the entire law is declared void.
        - 2. Basis of the Doctrine
            - Article 13 provides the constitutional basis for the doctrine of severability, with two key provisions:
                - 1. Article 13(1) addresses pre-Constitution laws, declaring them void to the extent they are inconsistent with Fundamental Rights.
                    - Article 13(1) states: "All laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void."
                - 2. Article 13(2) addresses post-Constitution laws, prohibiting the state from making laws that abridge Fundamental Rights, with such laws void to the extent of contravention.
                    - Article 13(2) states: "The State shall not make any law which takes away or abridges the rights conferred by this Part and any law made in contravention of this clause shall, to the extent of the contravention, be void."
            - Only the portion of a law violating Fundamental Rights is declared void, not the entire law.
            - The Supreme Court in R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla vs. Union of India (1957) clarified: "The question whether a statute which is void in part is to be treated as void in toto, or whether it is capable of enforcement as to that part which is valid… depends on whether what is valid could be separated from what is invalid."
        - 3. Propositions of the Doctrine
            - The Supreme Court in R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla vs. Union of India (1957) laid down the following propositions:
                - 1. The legislature's intention is the determining factor in assessing separability. The test is whether the legislature would have enacted the valid part had it known the rest was invalid.
                - 2. If valid and invalid provisions are inextricably mixed, the entire Act is invalid.
                - 3. If valid provisions are distinct but part of a single scheme intended to operate as a whole, the invalidity of a part invalidates the whole.
                - 4. If the valid part, after omitting the invalid, is so truncated as to differ in substance from the original, the entire law is rejected.
                - 5. Separability does not depend on whether provisions are in the same or different sections; the substance of the Act, examined as a whole, is material.
                - 6. If the remaining valid part cannot be enforced without judicial alterations, the entire law is void to avoid judicial legislation.
                - 7. Legislative intent on separability can be determined by considering the legislation's history, object, title, and preamble.
        - 4. Important Cases
            - 

    - Doctrine of Waiver
        - 1. Meaning of the Doctrine
            - The doctrine of waiver posits that a person entitled to a right or privilege may voluntarily relinquish it.
            - Surendra Malik and Sudeep Malik (Supreme Court on Doctrines and Maxims, 2014) define it as: "Waiver is an intentional relinquishment of a right. It involves conscious abandonment of an existing legal right, advantage, benefit, claim or privilege… There can be no waiver unless the person is fully informed as to his rights and with full knowledge, intentionally abandons them."
            - In India, the doctrine of waiver does not apply to Fundamental Rights; citizens cannot waive them. In contrast, in the USA, citizens may waive their fundamental rights, making India's position one of non-waiver.
        - 2. Position in India
            - The Supreme Court in Basheshar Nath vs. Commissioner of Income Tax (1958) observed:
                - 1. Fundamental Rights cannot be waived, as they are mandatory on the state to achieve Preamble objectives.
                - 2. The American doctrine of waiver cannot be applied to India's Constitution.
                - 3. Fundamental Rights are enshrined as public policy, not merely for individual benefit.
                - 4. Articles like 15(1), 20, and 21 make it clear citizens cannot waive protections (e.g., against discrimination or conviction).
                - 5. No distinction exists between rights for individual benefit and those for public policy, unlike in the USA.
                - 6. Given India's socio-economic and political context, the Supreme Court has a duty to safeguard Fundamental Rights.
        - 3. Important Cases
            - 

    - Doctrine of Eclipse
        - 1. Meaning of the Doctrine
            - The doctrine of eclipse arises from the prospective nature of Article 13(1), which declares pre-Constitution laws void to the extent they are inconsistent with Fundamental Rights.
            - Article 13(1) states: "All laws in force in the territory of India immediately before the commencement of this Constitution, in so far as they are inconsistent with the provisions of this Part, shall, to the extent of such inconsistency, be void."
            - A pre-Constitutional law inconsistent with a Fundamental Right is not void ab initio but becomes inoperative from January 26, 1950, overshadowed or eclipsed by the Fundamental Right. It remains dormant, not dead, and continues to exist for: (i) past transactions; (ii) rights and liabilities before 1950; (iii) non-citizens, who lack Fundamental Rights.
            - If a constitutional amendment removes the shadow, the law becomes enforceable again.
        - 2. Formulation of the Doctrine
            - The Supreme Court enunciated the doctrine in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras vs. State of M.P. (1955). Section 43 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939, amended in 1947, empowered the state to take over motor transport, but it became void in 1950 for violating Article 19(1)(g).
            - The 1st Amendment Act, 1951, amended Article 19(6), allowing state trade monopolies. A subsequent state notification was challenged, and the Court held that the law was eclipsed by the Fundamental Right until the amendment removed the shadow, reviving the law's validity.
        - 3. Application to Post-Constitutional Laws
            - Article 13(2) prohibits post-Constitution laws that abridge Fundamental Rights, declaring them void to the extent of contravention.
            - In Deep Chand vs. State of U.P. (1959) and Mahendra Lal Jain vs. State of U.P. (1962), the Court held that the doctrine of eclipse applies only to pre-Constitution laws, as post-Constitution laws violating Fundamental Rights are void ab initio and cannot be revived by amendment.
            - In State of Gujarat vs. Shri Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974), the Court reversed this, applying the doctrine to post-Constitution laws, holding they are not void for all purposes. A law violating Article 19 is valid for non-citizens, who lack Fundamental Rights.
            - In Dulare Lodh vs. IIIrd Additional District Judge, Kanpur (1984), the Court applied the doctrine to a post-Constitution law even against citizens.
        - 4. Important Cases
            - 1. Bhikaji Narain Dhakras vs. State of M.P. (1955)
            - 2. Deep Chand vs. State of U.P. (1959)
            - 3. Mahendra Lal Jain vs. State of U.P. (1962)
            - 4. State of Gujarat vs. Shri Ambica Mills Ltd. (1974)
            - 5. Dulare Lodh vs. IIIrd Additional District Judge, Kanpur (1984)

    - Doctrine of Territorial Nexus
        - 1. Meaning of the Doctrine
            - The doctrine of territorial nexus relates to Article 245, which delineates the legislative powers of Parliament and State Legislatures:
                - 1. Parliament can make laws for the whole or any part of India's territory and enact extra-territorial legislation, applying to Indian citizens and their property worldwide.
                - 2. State Legislatures can make laws for the whole or any part of the state but cannot enact extra-territorial legislation.
            - A State Legislature's law is generally not applicable outside the state, except when there is a sufficient nexus between the state and the object, as per the doctrine of territorial nexus.
            - The object need not be physically within the state, but there must be a real and sufficient connection between the state and the subject-matter.
        - 2. Formulation of the Doctrine
            - Pre-Constitution, the doctrine was applied in Governor-General vs. Raleigh Investment Company (1944), A.H. Wadia vs. Commissioner of Income-Tax (1949), and Wallace Brothers and Company Limited vs. Commissioner of Income-Tax (1948), all related to income-tax law.
            - Post-Constitution, the Supreme Court applied it in State of Bombay vs. R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla (1957), a case involving a tax on gambling. The Court held that a taxing law is valid if there is a sufficient territorial nexus, requiring: (i) a real, not illusory, nexus; (ii) liability relevant to that nexus.
            - In Tata Iron and Steel Company vs. State of Bihar (1958), the Court applied the doctrine to sales-tax law, noting it indicates when a tax is enforceable.
            - In State of A.P. vs. National Thermal Power Corporation Limited (2002), the Court clarified that extra-territorial state legislation is sustainable only with a sufficient and real territorial nexus.
        - 3. Application to Non-Tax Laws
            - The doctrine applies to non-tax laws, such as:
                - State of Bihar vs. Charusila Dasi (1959): The Court upheld a Bihar law on charitable and religious trusts, even if part of the trust property was in West Bengal, due to sufficient nexus.
                - Shrikant Bhalchandra Karulkar vs. State of Gujarat (1994): The Court upheld the Gujarat Agricultural Land Ceiling Act, 1960, which considered agricultural land held outside the state, as it had a sufficient nexus.
        - 4. Exceptions to the Doctrine
            - The doctrine does not apply in:
                - 1. State government schemes under the Motor Vehicles Act for inter-state routes, as in Khazan Singh vs. State of U.P. (1973).
                - 2. State trade and business under Article 298, which need not be restricted to state boundaries, as in Khazan Singh vs. State of U.P. (1973).
                
    - Doctrine of Pith and Substance
        - 1. Meaning of the Doctrine
            - Article 246 divides legislative powers between Parliament and State Legislatures via the Union List, State List, and Concurrent List in the Seventh Schedule.
            - The doctrine of pith and substance determines a law's validity by examining its true nature and character as an organic whole, not merely its sections.
            - If the pith and substance falls within the enacting legislature's domain, the law is valid, even if it incidentally encroaches on another legislature's sphere.
        - 2. Rationale of the Doctrine
            - Originating from Privy Council decisions in Canada and Australia, the doctrine addresses legislative competence in federal systems.
            - The Supreme Court in A.S. Krishna vs. State of Madras (1956) noted: "In a federal Constitution, some overlapping of legislative fields is inevitable due to the distribution of powers between the Centre and the Provinces."
        - 3. Principles of the Doctrine
            - Pre-Constitution, the Privy Council in Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee vs. Bank of Commerce (1947) applied the doctrine to the Bengal Money Lenders Act, 1946, holding it valid as its pith and substance was "money lending" (a state subject), despite incidental encroachment on "promissory notes" (a central subject).
            - The Privy Council laid down:
                - 1. Legislative powers overlap, requiring determination of the enactment's pith and substance and its appropriate list.
                - 2. The extent of invasion into another list is relevant to ascertain pith and substance, not validity.
                - 3. List I prevails over Lists III and II, and List III over List II, but the true character of the law determines its validity.
            - Post-Constitution, the Supreme Court consistently applied these principles.
        - 4. Important Cases
            - 

    - Doctrine of Colourable Legislation
        - 1. Meaning of the Doctrine
            - Article 246 and the Seventh Schedule divide legislative powers between Parliament and State Legislatures.
            - A law that appears within a legislature's competence but in substance exceeds it is void. Such a law, disguised to seem valid, is called colourable legislation.
            - The doctrine is based on the maxim: "You cannot do indirectly what you cannot do directly."
        - 2. Propositions of the Doctrine
            - The Supreme Court in K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo vs. State of Orissa (1953) laid down:
                - 1. Questions arise when a legislature transgresses its constitutional powers, whether overtly or covertly.
                - 2. Colourable legislation occurs when a legislature pretends to act within its powers but in reality exceeds them.
                - 3. The substance, not the form, determines validity.
                - 4. Constitutional prohibitions cannot be violated indirectly.
                - 5. The doctrine does not involve motives (bona fides or mala fides) but only legislative competence.
                - 6. Courts must scrutinize the statute's purpose and effect to ascertain its true nature, including related Acts if part of a scheme to evade constitutional provisions.
        - 3. Doctrine of Fraud on the Constitution
            - Colourable legislation is also known as fraud on the Constitution. In State of Bihar vs. Kameshwar Singh (1952), the Court described it as legislation ostensibly within constitutional powers but in reality outside them, covertly non-compliant.
        - 4. Doctrine of Fraud on Legislative Power
            - In S.S. Bola vs. B.D. Sardana (1997), the Court distinguished:
                - 1. Fraud on legislative power occurs when a legislature has power but pretends to exercise it, resulting in a non-law.
                - 2. Fraud on the Constitution occurs when a legislature lacks power but enacts a law in pretence, violating constitutional prohibitions.
                - 3. Fraud on legislative power applies to non-exercise of existing power; fraud on the Constitution applies to enactment despite prohibitions.
        - 5. Important Cases
            - 

    - Doctrine of Implied Powers
        - 1. Meaning of the Doctrine
            - Also known as the doctrine of implication, it holds that granting a power implies granting what is necessary for its exercise.
            - Black's Law Dictionary defines implied power as a political power not enumerated but necessary to carry out an express power.
            - Craies noted: "If a Legislature enables something to be done, it gives power by necessary implication to do everything indispensable for that purpose."
            - In Michael Fenton and James Fraser vs. John Stephen (1858), C.B. Pollock stated that anything authorized by law includes implied powers to do what is essential.
        - 2. Scope of the Doctrine
            - In Bidi, Bidi Leaves and Tobacco Merchants Association vs. State of Bombay (1961), the Supreme Court explained:
                - Implied powers are invoked when a statute imposes a duty or confers a power that cannot be exercised without auxiliary powers.
                - The impossibility must be general, rendering the statute unenforceable without implied powers.
        - 3. Application of the Doctrine
            - The Supreme Court applied the doctrine in:
                - Union of India vs. Gopal Chandra Misra (1978): A High Court judge has implied power under Article 217 to revoke resignation.
                - Rupa Ashok Hurra vs. Ashok Hurra (2002): The Court has implied power to reconsider judgments via curative petitions under Article 137.
                - Raja Ram Pal vs. Speaker of the Lok Sabha (2007): Parliament has implied power under Article 105 to expel members for contempt.
                - State of Punjab vs. Salil Sabhlok (2013): Article 316 implies the Governor's power to lay down procedures for State Public Service Commission appointments.
        - 4. Doctrine of Implied Prohibition
            - The opposite of implied powers, it holds that express mention of one thing excludes others.
            - Applied in the USA and Australia, where only central powers are enumerated, implying prohibition on central legislation for residuary subjects.
            - In India, both central and state powers are enumerated, so implied prohibition does not apply, though incidental powers do.

    - Doctrine of Incidental and Ancillary Powers
        - 1. Meaning of the Doctrine
            - Legislative powers in the Seventh Schedule carry incidental or ancillary powers necessary for their execution.
            - In the USA, these are "necessary and proper powers"; in Australia, "powers incidental to execution."
            - The American Constitution states Congress can make laws "necessary and proper" for executing its powers.
            - Justice Gajendragadkar observed: "Words conferring legislative power in the Constitution must receive liberal construction… extending to all ancillary matters reasonably included."
            - Examples: Power to levy tax includes preventing tax evasion (Commissioner of Commercial Taxes vs. R.S. Jhaver, 1967); power to collect rent includes remission of rent (United Provinces vs. Atiqa Begum, 1941).
            - Limits: Incidental powers cannot extend to unreasonable extents (e.g., tax power does not include confiscation, Check Post Officer vs. K.P. Abdulla, 1970) or cover subjects explicitly listed elsewhere (e.g., betting vs. tax on betting, R.M.D. Chamarbaugwalla vs. State of Mysore, 1961).
        - 2. Rationale of the Doctrine
            - In S.S. Bola vs. B.D. Sardana (1997), the Supreme Court noted that the doctrine validates laws by relieving them from unconstitutionality when they incidentally encroach on another legislative field but are substantially within competence.
            - Incidental encroachment is permissible if it does not substantially trespass into another field.
        - 3. Important Cases
            - 

    - Doctrine of Precedent
        - 1. Meaning of the Doctrine
            - The doctrine of precedent, or stare decisis, is an English principle where lower courts are bound by higher courts' decisions.
            - In Britain, all courts follow the House of Lords. In India, it ensures consistency and stability in judicial decisions.
            - The maxim "stare decisis et non quieta movere" means "to stand by decisions and not disturb what is settled."
            - Lord Coke stated: "Those things which have been so often adjudged ought to rest in peace."
            - In Shanker Raju vs. Union of India (2011), the Court emphasized maintaining settled judgments unless another view is compelling.
            - Former Chief Justice Chandrachud in Waman Rao vs. Union of India (1980) noted that stare decisis applies regardless of the decision's rationale.
        - 2. Basis of the Doctrine
            - Article 141 mandates that Supreme Court decisions are binding on all courts in India.
            - In Director of Settlements, A.P. vs. M.R. Apparao (2002), the Court held: "It is the duty of High Courts and subordinate courts to follow Supreme Court decisions… A High Court judgment refusing to follow the Supreme Court is a nullity."
            - In Suganathi Suresh Kumar vs. Jagdeeshan (2002), the Court emphasized judicial discipline under Article 141.
            - Courts adhere to precedents to maintain settled principles, as in Krishena Kumar vs. Union of India (1990).
        - 3. Rationale of the Doctrine
            - In Assistant Collector of Central Excise vs. Dunlop India Limited (1984), the Court noted that lower courts must loyally accept higher courts' decisions in a hierarchical system.
            - In Government of Andhra Pradesh vs. A.P. Jaiswal (2000), the Court stated: "Consistency is the cornerstone of justice… achieved through the rule of precedents."
            - In Union of India vs. Raghubir Singh (1989), the Court highlighted the doctrine's role in ensuring certainty and developing jurisprudence.
            - In Hari Singh vs. State of Haryana (1993), the Court warned against inconsistent opinions leading to judicial anarchy.
            - In Dwarikesh Sugar Industries Limited vs. Prem Heavy Engineering Works Limited (1997), the Court deprecated subordinate courts ignoring settled principles.
            - In Ganga Sugar Corporation vs. State of U.P. (1979), the Court noted that Supreme Court pronouncements are declaratory for the nation, with limited exceptions to stare decisis.

    - Doctrine of Occupied Field
        - 1. Meaning of the Doctrine
            - The doctrine of occupied field holds that when Parliament enacts a law on a subject, occupying the field, State Legislatures cannot legislate on that field.
            - Also known as the doctrine of covered field, it applies to Concurrent List entries under Article 254.
            - If a subject is in the Union List, State Legislatures are barred; if in the State List, Parliament is barred; if in the Concurrent List, both can legislate unless a central law occupies the field (Hindustan Lever vs. State of Maharashtra, 2003; State of Rajasthan vs. Vatan Medical and General Store, 2001).
        - 2. Doctrine of Repugnancy
            - Article 254 provides that if a parliamentary and state law on a Concurrent List subject are inconsistent, the parliamentary law prevails, and the state law is void to the extent of repugnancy.
            - In Deep Chand vs. State of U.P. (1959), the Supreme Court outlined repugnancy principles:
                - (i) Direct conflict between provisions.
                - (ii) Parliament's intent to create an exhaustive code.
                - (iii) Both laws occupying the same field.
            - In M. Karunanidhi vs. Union of India (1979), the Court laid down tests:
                - 1. Provisions must be inconsistent and irreconcilable.
                - 2. No implied repeal unless inconsistency is evident.
                - 3. If both laws can operate without collision, no repugnancy.
                - 4. If a statute creates distinct offences in the same field, both laws can coexist.
            - An exception under Article 254 allows a state law to prevail if reserved for the President's assent, though Parliament can supersede it.
        - 3. Repugnancy Outside the Concurrent List
            - In State of Kerala vs. Mar Appraem Kuri Company Limited (2012), the Court noted repugnancy arises when:
                - Laws in allotted spheres overlap and conflict, with parliamentary law prevailing under Article 246(1)'s non-obstante clause.
                - Laws on Concurrent List subjects conflict, with parliamentary law prevailing under Article 254(1).
            - In Hoechst Pharmaceuticals Limited vs. State of Bihar (1983), the Court clarified that Article 254(1) applies only to Concurrent List conflicts with direct inconsistency.

    - Doctrine of Prospective Overruling
        - 1. Meaning of the Doctrine
            - The doctrine of prospective overruling, originating in American jurisprudence, was first applied in India by the Supreme Court in I.C. Golak Nath vs. State of Punjab (1967).
            - When a court overrules a prior decision and announces a new ruling, it may restrict the new ruling's application to future transactions, preserving the validity of past transactions. This is known as prospective overruling.
            - The doctrine allows a court to overrule an old precedent (stare decisis) from a future date without retrospective effect.
            - In I.C. Golak Nath vs. State of Punjab (1967), the Supreme Court overruled its earlier decisions in Shankari S. Prasad vs. Union of India (1951) and Sajjan Singh vs. State of Rajasthan (1965). These cases held that Parliament's amending power under Article 368 includes the power to amend Fundamental Rights under Part III, and such amendments are not void under Article 13(2). In Golak Nath, the Court held that Article 368 cannot be used to abridge or take away Fundamental Rights, and a constitutional amendment is "law" under Article 13(2). The Court applied prospective overruling, declaring that this decision would operate prospectively, meaning Parliament would lack power to amend Part III from the date of the decision. The First Amendment Act (1951), Fourth Amendment Act (1955), and Seventeenth Amendment Act (1964) remained valid.
        - 2. Formulation of the Doctrine
            - In I.C. Golak Nath vs. State of Punjab (1967), the Supreme Court rejected the contention that prospective overruling constitutes judicial legislation. Explaining the Blackstonian theory (judges discover, not make, law) and the efficacy of prospective overruling, the Court observed:
                - "The doctrine of prospective overruling is a modern doctrine suitable for a fast-moving society. It does not do away with the doctrine of stare decisis but confines it to past transactions. While in strict theory, the doctrine may involve making law, the court declares the law but refuses to give retroactivity to it. It is a pragmatic solution reconciling the conflicting doctrines that a court finds and makes law. It finds the law but restricts its operation to the future. It enables the court to correct errors without disturbing past transactions. The court may prescribe the limits of retroactivity to mould relief to meet the ends of justice. By this doctrine, the past is preserved, and the future protected."
        - 3. Basis of the Doctrine
            - The Supreme Court outlined the legal and constitutional basis for prospective overruling:
                - "In India, there is no statutory prohibition against refusing retroactivity to declared law. The doctrine of res judicata precludes retroactivity for matters finally decided between parties. Courts reject retroactivity for statutory provisions affecting vested rights, and this case extends that rule. The Constitution does not expressly or by necessary implication oppose prospective overruling. Articles 32, 141, and 142 are couched in wide terms to enable the formulation of legal doctrines to meet justice’s ends, limited only by reason, restraint, and justice. Under Article 32, the Supreme Court can issue directions or writs to enforce Fundamental Rights. Article 141 makes Supreme Court declarations binding on all courts, and Article 142 allows orders necessary for complete justice. These articles enable the Supreme Court to declare law and issue directions. The term 'declared' is broader than 'found' or 'made,' encompassing interpretation and evolution. The law declared superseding earlier law can be restricted to future operation, preserving past transactions. Denying this power on the theory that courts only find law undermines the judiciary’s role as an instrument of justice."
        - 4. Propositions of the Doctrine
            - The Supreme Court in I.C. Golak Nath vs. State of Punjab (1967) laid down three propositions:
                - 1. The doctrine of prospective overruling applies only to matters arising under the Constitution.
                - 2. It can be invoked only by the Supreme Court, as it has constitutional jurisdiction to declare law binding on all courts in India.
                - 3. The scope of retroactive operation of the law declared, superseding earlier decisions, is at the Supreme Court’s discretion, moulded to suit the justice of the case.
        - 5. Rationale of the Doctrine
            - The Supreme Court explained the rationale in I.C. Golak Nath vs. State of Punjab (1967):
                - "We conclude that: (1) Parliament has no power to amend Part III to abridge Fundamental Rights; (2) this case warrants prospective overruling. Considering the history of amendments, their socio-economic impact, and the chaos from sudden withdrawal, judicial restraint is needed. We declare that our decision will not affect the validity of the Constitution (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964, or other amendments abridging Fundamental Rights. Parliament will have no power to amend Part III to abridge Fundamental Rights in the future."
            - In Baburao vs. C.C. Jacob (1999), the Court observed:
                - 1. Prospective declaration avoids reopening settled issues and prevents multiple proceedings.
                - 2. It reduces uncertainty and avoidable litigation.
                - 3. Actions contrary to the declared law before its declaration are validated in the public interest.
        - 6. Criticism of the Doctrine
            - The Supreme Court addressed objections in I.C. Golak Nath vs. State of Punjab (1967):
                - "Objections include: (1) the doctrine involves judicial legislation; (2) it discourages appeals, as parties gain no benefit; (3) future declarations are obiter; (4) it is undesirable; (5) retroactivity curbs facile overruling. These are not insurmountable. If a court can overrule prior decisions, it can restrict rulings to the future. Even if a party does not benefit, future appeals under the new law will. The decision is not obiter, as the court declares law with restricted scope. Stability in law does not perpetuate injustice."
        - 7. Continuation of the Doctrine
            - Although I.C. Golak Nath vs. State of Punjab (1967) was overruled in Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala (1973), the doctrine of prospective overruling was upheld and applied in subsequent cases.
            - The doctrine was extended to matters under ordinary statutes.
            - In Indra Sawhney vs. Union of India (1992), the Court postponed operation of its judgment for five years, exemplifying prospective overruling.
            - In Managing Director, ECIL, Hyderabad vs. B. Karunakar (1993), the Court limited benefits to pending cases from the judgment date, excluding prior actions.

    - Doctrine of Harmonious Construction
        - 1. Meaning of the Doctrine
            - The doctrine of harmonious construction, also known as the rule of avoidance of conflict, requires courts to interpret conflicting constitutional provisions harmoniously to avoid conflictual implications.
            - Justice Venkataramana Aiyar in Sri Venkataramana Devaru vs. State of Mysore (1958) observed: "In case of two irreconcilable provisions, they should be interpreted to give effect to both, rendering neither nugatory."
            - Justice B.K. Mukherjea in A.K. Gopalan vs. State of Madras (1950) stated: "If constitutional provisions appear in conflict, they should be reconciled to give effect to all, if possible."
            - Key points:
                - 1. The Constitution should be read as a whole, considering all parts.
                - 2. Courts presume the Constitution-makers intended no conflict between parts.
        - 2. Application of the Doctrine
            - The Supreme Court applied the doctrine to reconcile conflicts between:
                - 1. Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles of State Policy.
                - 2. Different Fundamental Rights.
                - 3. Fundamental Rights and legislative privileges.
                - 4. Fundamental Rights and amendment procedures.
                - 5. Fundamental Rights and other constitutional parts.
                - 6. Different entries in the Seventh Schedule’s legislative lists.
            - In Ranjana Dwivedi vs. Union of India (1983), the Court observed on Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles: "Early decisions paid little regard to directives, as they were non-justiciable, unlike Fundamental Rights. Later decisions, culminating in Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala (1973), emphasized courts’ duty to harmonize directives and Fundamental Rights, as both aim for social revolution and a welfare state per the Preamble. Courts must ensure directives’ implementation while harmonizing with individual rights."
            - On Seventh Schedule entries, the Court in Calcutta Gas Co. vs. State of West Bengal (1962) stated: "Entries should be given the widest amplitude, but overlapping or conflicting entries require reconciliation. Courts must harmonize entries to give effect to all. Only when reconciliation is impossible does the Union’s overriding power, via the non-obstante clause, prevail."
        - 3. Important Cases
            - 

    - Doctrine of Liberal Interpretation
        - 1. Meaning of the Doctrine
            - The doctrine of liberal interpretation requires the Constitution to be interpreted broadly and liberally, not narrowly or pedantically.
            - It views the Constitution not as mere law but as a framework for law-making, assuming it is a living, organic entity requiring broad interpretation.
            - Justice Higgins in Attorney-General for New South Wales vs. Brewery Employees Union (1908) observed: "While we interpret constitutional words like ordinary laws, these principles compel us to consider the Constitution’s nature as a mechanism for law-making, not a mere Act declaring law."
            - In Life Insurance Corporation of India vs. Manubhai D. Shah (1992), the Supreme Court stated: "A constitutional provision is ever-evolving, not static, and does not admit a narrow, pedantic, or syllogistic approach. Constitutional provisions, especially Fundamental Rights, require broad interpretation, not restricted approaches."
            - For Seventh Schedule entries, the Court in Elektro Hotels GmbH & Investments Ltd. vs. Union of India (1989) observed: "Entries in legislative lists should not be read narrowly. Each general word extends to ancillary or subsidiary matters reasonably included. Words in a constitutional document conferring legislative power receive the widest construction, per their ordinary meaning, to have effect in their fullest amplitude."
        - 2. Doctrine of Literal Interpretation
            - Also known as strict or positivist construction, the doctrine of literal interpretation requires constitutional provisions to be interpreted in their plain, ordinary, natural, and grammatical meaning.
            - Justice B.K. Mukherjea in Chiranjit Lal Chowdhuri vs. Union of India (1950) stated: "We should interpret the Constitution by the plain words used by its makers."
            - In A.K. Gopalan vs. State of Madras (1950), the Court observed: "Courts cannot declare an Act void based on a supposed spirit not expressed in words. Where the Constitution does not limit legislative powers, courts cannot impose limitations based on an unexpressed spirit. Judicial interpretation cannot limit sovereign legislative power except as authorized by the Constitution’s express words."
            - In In re Sea Customs Act (1963), the Court held: "The Constitution must be interpreted by its terms alone, without reading in supposed spirits, policy, or corrections for omissions."
        - 3. Doctrine of Purposive Interpretation
            - The doctrine of purposive interpretation requires courts to consider the purpose behind a constitutional provision, ascertaining the Constitution-makers’ intent.
            - The Preamble and Constituent Assembly Debates illuminate provisions’ purposes. Sir Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar, a Drafting Committee member, stated: "The Preamble expresses what we had thought or dreamt so long."
            - In In re Berubari Union (1960), the Supreme Court held: "The Preamble is a key to the minds of the Constitution-makers."
            - In S.R. Chaudhuri vs. State of Punjab (2001), the Court observed: "Constitutional provisions require an object-oriented approach, not a narrow or pedantic construction. Their full import must be appreciated in context and purpose."
            - Former Chief Justice J.S. Verma in New Dimensions of Justice (2000) stated: "The Constitution is a living, vibrant organism for current societal needs, construed as enacting concepts. Constitutional purpose must guide interpretation."
        - 4. Doctrine of Creative Interpretation
            - The doctrine of creative interpretation envisages innovative judicial interpretation to evolve new concepts and procedures for changing situations.
            - In I.C. Golak Nath vs. State of Punjab (1967), the Supreme Court introduced the American doctrine of prospective overruling, allowing overruling of precedents from a future date without retrospective effect.
            - The Court observed: "Articles 32, 141, and 142 enable the Court to formulate legal doctrines for justice. Denying this power based on the theory that courts only find law undermines the judiciary’s role as an instrument of justice."
            - In Kesavananda Bharati vs. State of Kerala (1973), the Court innovated the doctrine of the basic structure of the Constitution, a landmark in judicial creativity in India.


- Chapter 92: World Constitutions
    - American Constitution
        - The American Constitution is the Constitution of the United States of America which was formed in 1787 following the American Revolution (1775–1783). The Constitution was adopted in 1787 at the Philadelphia Convention and came into force in 1789. The salient features of the American Constitution are explained as follows:
            - 1. Written Constitution
                - The American Constitution is usually cited as a classic example of a written Constitution. In fact, it is the oldest among the existing written Constitutions of the world. It is contained in a document of some 12 pages and consists of a Preamble, 7 Articles and 27 Amendments.
            - 2. Rigid Constitution
                - Unlike the British Constitution, the American Constitution is a rigid one. It cannot be amended by the Congress in the same manner as the ordinary laws are made. It can be amended by the Congress only by means of a special process provided by the Constitution for that purpose. Therefore, in the USA, there exists a distinction between a constitutional law and an ordinary law.
                - The American Constitution, the most rigid constitution in the world, lays down the following two methods for its amendment:
                    - (i) An amendment can be proposed by two-third votes of both the Houses of the Congress. It should be ratified by the legislatures of three-fourths (38 out of 50) of the states within a seven-year time span.
                    - (ii) Alternatively, an amendment can be proposed by a constitutional convention called by the Congress on the petition of two-thirds (34 out of 50) of the state legislatures. It should be ratified by the convention in three-fourths (38 out of 50) of state legislatures.
                - Hence, the procedure prescribed by the American Constitution for its amendment is very difficult, complicated and slow. Its rigid character is evident from the fact that it has been amended only 27 times since its promulgation in 1789.
            - 3. Federal Constitution
                - USA is a federal state. In fact, the USA is the first and the oldest federal state in the modern world. It is a federal republic comprising 50 states (originally 13 states) and the District of Columbia. The Constitution provides for division of powers between the Federal (Central) Government and the State Governments. It confers limited and specified powers on the Centre and vests the residuary powers (which are not enumerated in the Constitution) in the States. Each state has its own Constitution, elected legislature, governor and Supreme Court.
            - 4. Presidential Government
                - Unlike the British Constitution, the American Constitution provides for the Presidential form of Government. The features of the American Presidential system of Government are as follows:
                    - (i) The American President is both, the head of State and the head of Government. As the head of State, he/she occupies a ceremonial position. As the head of Government, he/she leads the executive organ of Government. The President of the USA is the chief real executive.
                    - (ii) The President is elected by an electoral college for a fixed tenure of four years. He/she cannot be removed by the Congress except by impeachment for a grave unconstitutional act.
                    - (iii) The President governs with the help of the Cabinet or a smaller body called ‘Kitchen’ Cabinet. It is only an advisory body and consists of non-elected departmental secretaries. They are selected and appointed by him/her and are responsible only to him/her. They can also be removed by him/her any time.
                    - (iv) The President and his/her Secretaries are not responsible to the Congress for their acts. They neither possess membership in the Congress nor attend its sessions.
                    - (v) The President cannot dissolve the House of Representatives—the lower House of the Congress.
            - 5. Separation of Powers
                - The doctrine of separation of powers is the basis of the American constitutional system. The legislative, executive and judicial powers of the Government are separated and vested in the three independent organs of the Government. The first three articles of the Constitution clearly manifest this feature of the Constitution. Article I says that all legislative powers herein granted shall be vested in the Congress. Article II states that the executive powers shall be vested in the President. Article III provides that the judicial powers shall be vested in one Supreme Court and in such inferior courts as the Congress may from time to time ordain and establish.
            - 6. Checks and Balances
                - The system of checks and balances in the American Constitution is an outcome of the adoption of the principle of separation of powers. It enables each organ of the Government to exercise partial control on others so that no organ becomes autocratic and irresponsible. This means that no organ of Government has unrestricted powers even in its own sphere.
                - Some aspects of the working of the system of checks and balances in the American Constitutional system are:
                    - (i) The President can veto the bills passed by the Congress. He/she enjoys two kinds of vetoes—Pocket veto and Qualified veto.
                    - (ii) The Senate confirms the higher appointments made and international treaties concluded by the President.
                    - (iii) The Congress determines the organisation and appellate jurisdiction of the judiciary.
                    - (iv) The President appoints the judges with the consent of the Senate.
                    - (v) The Supreme Court can declare the congressional laws and Presidential orders as ultra vires.
            - 7. Supremacy of Constitution and Judicial Review
                - The American Constitution embodies the principle of ‘hierarchy of laws’. The written Constitution is regarded as the highest (supreme or fundamental) law of the land. The statutes of the Congress and state legislatures must conform to this supreme law. If these statutes are against the provisions of the Constitution, they can be declared by the Supreme Court as ultra vires (and hence, null and void). The Supreme Court thus acts as the custodian of the Constitution through its power of judicial review.
            - 8. Bill of Rights
                - The American Constitution is the first Constitution in the world to carry the Bill of Rights. It guarantees a large number of rights to the people. It says that no person is to be deprived of life, liberty and property without due process of law. These rights impose restrictions on the authority of the Government. The Supreme Court acts as the protector of these rights through its power of judicial review. This Bill of Rights was added to the original Constitution in 1791 through the first ten amendments.
            - 9. Bicameralism
                - The American Federal Legislature called the Congress is bicameral, that is, it consists of two Houses, namely the Senate and the House of Representatives. The Senate is the upper House while the House of Representatives is the lower House. The Senate consists of 100 members, two being elected from each state to serve for a fixed six-year term. The House of Representatives consists of 435 members elected from single member constituencies to serve for a fixed two-year term. The Senate is the more powerful chamber of the Congress. In fact, the American Senate is the most powerful second chamber (upper House) in the world.
        - American President
            - Mode of Election
                - The American Constitution provides for an indirect election of the President. However, the growth of political parties and political conventions has converted it into a direct election. Constitutionally, the President is elected by an electoral college constituted for the purpose. The members of this college (called as Presidential Electors) are elected directly by the people of all the states. The number of Presidential electors in each state is equal to the number of its members in the Congress (both in the House of Representatives and in the Senate). It means that the electoral college consists of as many members as is the total strength of the two Houses of the Congress. Additionally, three votes have been given to the District of Columbia, a federal enclave and not a state. Thus, the total strength of the electoral college is 538 (435 is the strength of the House of Representatives, 100 is the strength of the Senate and three members of the District of Columbia). A candidate in order to win the Presidential election needs 270 votes, that is, 269 (half of the total votes of 538) plus one.
                - It must be stressed here that the members of the electoral college are not the members of the Congress. The college is a special body which is formed only for electing the President and it gets dissolved after this. If no candidate secures the requisite majority, the House of Representatives elects the President from among the three candidates securing the highest votes in the electoral college. There have been three such occasions (1800, 1824 and 1876).
            - Qualifications, Term and Removal
                - According to the Constitution, a candidate for the presidency must have the following three qualifications:
                    - (i) He/she must be a natural born citizen of the USA. A naturalised citizen is not eligible.
                    - (ii) He/she must have attained the age of thirty-five years.
                    - (iii) He/she must have been a resident of the USA for fourteen years (not necessarily consecutive).
                - The President holds the office for a fixed tenure of four years. He/she is eligible for re-election but only once. The 22nd Amendment Act of 1951 has fixed the maximum total term for any President at ten years. In other words, it bars any person from being elected as President more than twice. The Presidential term of four years begins on 20th January.
                - The President may be removed from the office before the expiry of his/her normal tenure of four years through impeachment for treason, bribery or other high crimes and misdemeanors. The House of Representatives initiates the impeachment proceedings by a majority vote. The case is then tried by the Senate. During this trial period, the Senate acts as a judicial tribunal and is presided over by the chief justice of the Supreme Court (and not the vice-President). If the Senate also passes the impeachment resolution by a two-thirds majority, the President stands impeached. So far, no American President has ever been removed by impeachment. However, there have been five impeachment attempts—Andrew Johnson (1868), Richard Nixon (1974), Bill Clinton (1998), Donald Trump (first time in 2019) and Donald Trump (second time in 2021).
            - Powers and Functions
                - The American presidency is one of the strongest democratic offices in the world. Lord Bryce regards it as ‘the greatest office in the world’. Munro observed, “the American President exercises the largest amount of authority ever wielded by any man in a democracy”. Ogg regards him/her as “the greatest ruler of the world”. Harold Laski remarked, “the President of the United States is both more and less than a King, he/she is also both more and less than a Prime Minister”.
                - The President derives his/her powers and functions from four sources: Constitution, statutes of Congress, judicial interpretations and political conventions. These are mentioned below:
                    - 1. He/she has to enforce the Constitution, federal laws and treaties, and judicial decisions throughout the country.
                    - 2. He/she is the supreme commander of the armed forces of the US.
                    - 3. He/she appoints the Supreme Court judges, ambassadors, heads of executive departments, diplomatic officials, consuls and other top officials.
                    - 4. He/she formulates foreign policy and conducts foreign affairs of the US.
                    - 5. He/she can grant pardon and reprieve for offences against federal laws (except in cases of impeachment).
                    - 6. When a bill approved by both the Houses of the Congress is sent to him/her for his/her assent, he/she has three options before him/her:
                        - (i) He/she may give his/her assent to the bill and the bill then becomes an Act.
                        - (ii) He/she may reject the bill and return it to the Congress within ten days. However, if the same bill is re-passed by the Congress by a two-thirds majority, then the bill becomes a law and the President has to sign it. This is known as ‘Qualified Veto’.
                        - (iii) He/she may reserve the bill with him/her. Then, the bill becomes a law after the expiry of ten days without his/her assent. However, if the Congress ends the session before ten days, then the bill automatically dies. This is known as ‘Pocket Veto’.
                    - 7. He/she can send messages to the Congress proposing some legislative measures; either orally delivered to the House or sent in the form of a document.
                    - 8. He/she can call special sessions of the Congress for consideration of urgent matters.
                    - 9. He/she prepares the national budget and submits it to the Congress for approval.
                    - 10. He/she is empowered to make rules and regulations in the form of executive orders. This is known as delegated legislation.
