- Appendix IV: Constitutional Amendments at a Glance
- Appendix V: Constitutional Amendments with Reference to Articles (Combined)
    - The following provides a summary of the constitutional amendments made to the Constitution of India, highlighting key provisions and the specific articles amended, added, or repealed:
        - 1. First Amendment Act, 1951
            - Empowered the state to make special provisions for the advancement of socially and economically backward classes.
            - Provided for the saving of laws providing for acquisition of estates, etc.
            - Added Ninth Schedule to protect land reform and other laws included in it from judicial review.
            - Added three more grounds of restrictions on freedom of speech and expression, viz., public order, friendly relations with foreign states, and incitement to an offence. Also made the restrictions ‘reasonable’ and thus justiciable.
            - Provided that state trading and nationalisation of any trade or business by the state is not invalid on the ground of violation of the right to trade or business.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 15, 19, 31, 31A, 31B.
                - Added Ninth Schedule.
        - 2. Second Amendment Act, 1952
            - Readjusted the scale of representation in the Lok Sabha by providing that one member could represent even more than 7,50,000 persons.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 81.
        - 3. Third Amendment Act, 1954
            - Empowered the Parliament to control the production, supply, and distribution of foodstuffs, cattle fodder, raw cotton, cotton seed, and raw jute in the public interest.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Seventh Schedule (Entry 33, List III).
        - 4. Fourth Amendment Act, 1955
            - Made the scale of compensation given in lieu of compulsory acquisition of private property beyond the scrutiny of courts.
            - Authorised the state to nationalise any trade.
            - Included some more Acts in the Ninth Schedule.
            - Extended the scope of Article 31A (saving of laws).
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 31, 31A, Ninth Schedule.
        - 5. Fifth Amendment Act, 1955
            - Empowered the President to fix the time limit for the state legislatures to express their views on proposed Central legislation affecting the areas, boundaries, and names of the states.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 3.
        - 6. Sixth Amendment Act, 1956
            - Included a new subject in the Union List, i.e., taxes on the sale and purchase of goods in the course of inter-state trade and commerce, and restricted the state’s power in this regard.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 269, 286, Seventh Schedule (Entries 92, 92A, List I; Entry 54, List II).
        - 7. Seventh Amendment Act, 1956
            - Abolished the existing classification of states into four categories, i.e., Part A, Part B, Part C, and Part D states, and reorganised them into 14 states and 6 union territories.
            - Extended the jurisdiction of high courts to union territories.
            - Provided for the establishment of a common high court for two or more states.
            - Provided for the appointment of additional and acting judges of the high court.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 1, 3, 49, 80, 81, 82, 131, 153, 158, 168, 170, 171, 216, 217, 220, 222, 224, 230, 231, 232, 239, 240, 241, 258A, First Schedule, Second Schedule, Seventh Schedule.
                - Repealed Articles 238, 242, 243.
        - 8. Eighth Amendment Act, 1960
            - Extended the reservation of seats for the Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), and special representation for Anglo-Indians in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies for a period of ten years (i.e., up to 1970).
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 334, 335.
        - 9. Ninth Amendment Act, 1960
            - Facilitated the cession of Indian territory of Berubari Union (located in West Bengal) to Pakistan as provided in the Indo-Pakistan Agreement (1958).
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended First Schedule.
        - 10. Tenth Amendment Act, 1961
            - Incorporated Dadra and Nagar Haveli in the Indian Union.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 240, First Schedule.
        - 11. Eleventh Amendment Act, 1961
            - Changed the procedure for election of the Vice-President by providing for an electoral college instead of a joint meeting of the two Houses of Parliament.
            - Provided that the election of the President or Vice-President cannot be challenged on the ground of any vacancy in the appropriate electoral college.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 66, 71.
        - 12. Twelfth Amendment Act, 1962
            - Incorporated Goa, Daman, and Diu in the Indian Union.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 240, First Schedule.
        - 13. Thirteenth Amendment Act, 1962
            - Gave the status of a state to Nagaland and made special provisions for it.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 170, added Article 371A.
        - 14. Fourteenth Amendment Act, 1962
            - Incorporated Puducherry in the Indian Union.
            - Provided for the creation of legislatures and councils of ministers for the Union Territories of Himachal Pradesh, Manipur, Tripura, Goa, Daman and Diu, and Puducherry.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 81, 240, First Schedule, added Articles 239A, 239B.
        - 15. Fifteenth Amendment Act, 1963
            - Enabled the high courts to issue writs to any person or authority even outside their territorial jurisdiction if the cause of action arises within their territorial limits.
            - Increased the retirement age of high court judges from 60 to 62 years.
            - Provided for the appointment of retired judges of high courts as acting judges of the same court.
            - Provided for compensatory allowance to judges transferred from one high court to another.
            - Enabled a retired judge of a high court to act as an ad hoc judge of the Supreme Court.
            - Provided for the procedure for determining the age of Supreme Court and high court judges.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 124, 128, 217, 222, 224, 226, 297, 311, 316.
        - 16. Sixteenth Amendment Act, 1963
            - Empowered the state to impose further restrictions on the rights to freedom of speech and expression, to assemble peaceably, and to form associations in the interests of sovereignty and integrity of India.
            - Included sovereignty and integrity in the forms of oaths or affirmations to be subscribed by candidates to legislatures, members of legislatures, ministers, judges, and the Comptroller and Auditor General of India.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 19, 84, 173, Third Schedule.
        - 17. Seventeenth Amendment Act, 1964
            - Prohibited the acquisition of land under personal cultivation unless the market value of the land is paid as compensation.
            - Included 44 more Acts in the Ninth Schedule.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 31A, Ninth Schedule.
        - 18. Eighteenth Amendment Act, 1966
            - Made it clear that the power of Parliament to form a new state also includes the power to form a new state or union territory by uniting a part of a state or a union territory to another state or union territory.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 3.
        - 19. Nineteenth Amendment Act, 1966
            - Abolished the system of Election Tribunals and vested the power to hear election petitions in the High Courts.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 324.
        - 20. Twentieth Amendment Act, 1966
            - Validated certain appointments of district judges in Uttar Pradesh which were declared void by the Supreme Court.
            - Amended Articles
                - Added Article 233A.
        - 21. Twenty-First Amendment Act, 1967
            - Included Sindhi as the 15th language in the Eighth Schedule.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Eighth Schedule.
        - 22. Twenty-Second Amendment Act, 1969
            - Facilitated the creation of an autonomous state of Meghalaya within the state of Assam.
            - Amended Articles
                - Added Articles 244A, 371B.
        - 23. Twenty-Third Amendment Act, 1969
            - Extended the reservation of seats for the SCs, STs, and special representation for Anglo-Indians in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies for a further period of ten years (i.e., up to 1980).
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 333, 334.
        - 24. Twenty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1971
            - Affirmed the power of Parliament to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.
            - Made it compulsory for the President to give assent to a Constitutional Amendment Bill.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 13, 368.
        - 25. Twenty-Fifth Amendment Act, 1971
            - Curtailed the fundamental right to property.
            - Provided that any law made to give effect to the Directive Principles contained in Article 39(b) or (c) cannot be challenged on the ground of violation of the rights guaranteed by Articles 14, 19, and 31.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 31, 31C.
        - 26. Twenty-Sixth Amendment Act, 1971
            - Abolished the privy purses and privileges of the former rulers of princely states.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 366, 363A, repealed Article 291.
        - 27. Twenty-Seventh Amendment Act, 1971
            - Empowered administrators of certain union territories to promulgate ordinances.
            - Made special provisions for the new Union Territories of Arunachal Pradesh and Mizoram.
            - Authorised Parliament to create a legislative assembly and council of ministers for the new state of Manipur.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 239A, 240, added Articles 239B, 371C.
        - 28. Twenty-Eighth Amendment Act, 1972
            - Abolished the special privileges of ICS officers and empowered Parliament to determine their service conditions.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 312, repealed Article 314.
        - 29. Twenty-Ninth Amendment Act, 1972
            - Included two Kerala Acts on land reforms in the Ninth Schedule.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Ninth Schedule.
        - 30. Thirtieth Amendment Act, 1972
            - Did away with the provision allowing appeals to the Supreme Court in civil cases involving an amount of Rs. 20,000, and provided instead that an appeal can be filed only if the case involves a substantial question of law.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 133.
        - 31. Thirty-First Amendment Act, 1973
            - Increased the number of Lok Sabha seats from 525 to 545.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 81, 82, 170, 330, 332.
        - 32. Thirty-Second Amendment Act, 1973
            - Made special provisions to satisfy the aspirations of the people of the Telangana region in Andhra Pradesh.
            - Amended Articles
                - Added Article 371D.
        - 33. Thirty-Third Amendment Act, 1974
            - Provided that the resignation of members of Parliament and state legislatures may be accepted by the Speaker/Chairman only if satisfied that the resignation is voluntary or genuine.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 101, 190.
        - 34. Thirty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1974
            - Included 20 more land tenure and land reform Acts of various states in the Ninth Schedule.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Ninth Schedule.
        - 35. Thirty-Fifth Amendment Act, 1974
            - Terminated the protectorate status of Sikkim and conferred on it the status of an associate state of the Indian Union. Added the Tenth Schedule laying down the terms and conditions of association of Sikkim with the Indian Union.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 80, 81, added Tenth Schedule.
        - 36. Thirty-Sixth Amendment Act, 1975
            - Made Sikkim a full-fledged state of the Indian Union and omitted the Tenth Schedule.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 80, 81, First Schedule, repealed Tenth Schedule.
        - 37. Thirty-Seventh Amendment Act, 1975
            - Provided for a legislative assembly and council of ministers for the Union Territory of Arunachal Pradesh.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 239A, 240.
        - 38. Thirty-Eighth Amendment Act, 1975
            - Made the declaration of emergency by the President non-justiciable.
            - Made the promulgation of ordinances by the President, Governors, and administrators of union territories non-justiciable.
            - Empowered the President to declare different proclamations of national emergency on different grounds simultaneously.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 123, 213, 239B, 352, 356, 357, 360.
        - 39. Thirty-Ninth Amendment Act, 1975
            - Placed disputes relating to the President, Vice-President, Prime Minister, and Speaker beyond the scope of the judiciary, to be decided by an authority determined by Parliament.
            - Included certain Central Acts in the Ninth Schedule.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 71, added Article 329A, amended Ninth Schedule.
        - 40. Fortieth Amendment Act, 1976
            - Empowered Parliament to specify from time to time the limits of territorial waters, the continental shelf, the exclusive economic zone (EEZ), and maritime zones of India.
            - Included 64 more Central and state laws, mostly relating to land reforms, in the Ninth Schedule.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 297, 312, Ninth Schedule.
        - 41. Forty-First Amendment Act, 1976
            - Raised the retirement age of members of State Public Service Commissions and Joint Public Service Commissions from 60 to 62.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 316.
        - 42. Forty-Second Amendment Act, 1976 (Popularly known as the ‘Mini-Constitution’)
            - Added three new words (Socialist, Secular, Integrity) to the Preamble.
            - Added Fundamental Duties of citizens (new Part IVA).
            - Made the President bound by the advice of the Council of Ministers.
            - Provided for administrative tribunals and tribunals for other matters (added Part XIVA).
            - Froze the seats in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies on the basis of the 1971 census till 2001.
            - Made constitutional amendments beyond judicial scrutiny.
            - Curtailed the power of judicial review and writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and high courts.
            - Raised the tenure of Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies from 5 to 6 years.
            - Provided that laws made for the implementation of Directive Principles cannot be declared invalid by courts on the ground of violation of some Fundamental Rights.
            - Empowered Parliament to make laws to deal with anti-national activities, with such laws taking precedence over Fundamental Rights.
            - Added three new Directive Principles: equal justice and free legal aid, participation of workers in the management of industries, and protection of environment, forests, and wildlife.
            - Facilitated the proclamation of national emergency in a part of the territory of India.
            - Extended the one-time duration of President’s Rule in a state from 6 months to one year.
            - Empowered the Centre to deploy its armed forces in any state to deal with a grave situation of law and order.
            - Shifted five subjects from the State List to the Concurrent List: education, forests, protection of wild animals and birds, weights and measures, and administration of justice, constitution, and organisation of all courts except the Supreme Court and high courts.
            - Did away with the requirement of a quorum in Parliament and state legislatures.
            - Empowered Parliament to decide from time to time the rights and privileges of its members and committees.
            - Provided for the creation of the All-India Judicial Service.
            - Shortened the procedure for disciplinary action by taking away the right of a civil servant to make representation at the second stage after the inquiry (i.e., on the penalty proposed).
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Preamble, Articles 31C, 39, 48A, 51A, 55, 74, 77, 81, 82, 83, 100, 102, 103, 105, 118, 145, 166, 170, 172, 189, 191, 192, 194, 208, 225, 227, 228, 311, 312, 330, 352, 353, 356, 357, 358, 359, 366, 368, Seventh Schedule.
                - Added Parts IVA, XIVA, Articles 239AA, 323A, 323B.
        - 43. Forty-Third Amendment Act, 1977 (Enacted by the Janata Government to nullify some distortions introduced by the 42nd Amendment)
            - Restored the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and high courts in respect of judicial review and issue of writs.
            - Deprived Parliament of its special powers to make laws to deal with anti-national activities.
            - Amended Articles
                - Repealed Article 31D, amended Articles 145, 226, 228A, 366.
        - 44. Forty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1978 (Enacted by the Janata Government to nullify some distortions introduced by the 42nd Amendment)
            - Restored the original term of the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies (i.e., 5 years).
            - Restored the provisions with regard to quorum in Parliament and state legislatures.
            - Omitted the reference to the British House of Commons in provisions pertaining to parliamentary privileges.
            - Gave constitutional protection to publication in newspapers of true reports of the proceedings of Parliament and state legislatures.
            - Empowered the President to send back the advice of the Council of Ministers once for reconsideration, but the reconsidered advice is binding.
            - Deleted the provision that made the satisfaction of the President, Governor, and administrators final in issuing ordinances.
            - Restored some powers of the Supreme Court and high courts.
            - Replaced the term ‘internal disturbance’ with ‘armed rebellion’ in respect of national emergency.
            - Made the President declare a national emergency only on the written recommendation of the Cabinet.
            - Made certain procedural safeguards with respect to national emergency and President’s Rule.
            - Deleted the right to property from the list of Fundamental Rights and made it a legal right.
            - Provided that the Fundamental Rights guaranteed by Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended during a national emergency.
            - Omitted provisions that took away the power of courts to decide election disputes of the President, Vice-President, Prime Minister, and Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 19, 22, 30, 31A, 31C, 38, 71, 74, 77, 83, 103, 123, 132, 134, 139A, 150, 166, 172, 192, 194, 213, 217, 225, 226, 227, 239B, 329, 352, 356, 358, 359, 360, 366, 368.
                - Repealed Articles 31, 257A, 329A.
        - 45. Forty-Fifth Amendment Act, 1980
            - Extended the reservation of seats for the SCs, STs, and special representation for Anglo-Indians in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies for a further period of ten years (i.e., up to 1990).
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 334.
        - 46. Forty-Sixth Amendment Act, 1982
            - Enabled states to plug loopholes in laws and realise sales tax dues.
            - Brought about some uniformity in tax rates on certain items.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 269, 286, 366, Seventh Schedule.
        - 47. Forty-Seventh Amendment Act, 1984
            - Included 14 land reform Acts of various states in the Ninth Schedule.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Ninth Schedule.
        - 48. Forty-Eighth Amendment Act, 1984
            - Facilitated the extension of President’s Rule in Punjab beyond one year without meeting the two special conditions for such extension.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 356.
        - 49. Forty-Ninth Amendment Act, 1984
            - Gave constitutional sanctity to the Autonomous District Council in Tripura.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 244, Fifth Schedule.
        - 50. Fiftieth Amendment Act, 1984
            - Empowered Parliament to restrict the Fundamental Rights of persons employed in intelligence organisations and telecommunication systems set up for the armed forces or intelligence organisations.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 33.
        - 51. Fifty-First Amendment Act, 1984
            - Provided for reservation of seats in the Lok Sabha for STs in Meghalaya, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, and Mizoram, as well as in the legislative assemblies of Meghalaya and Nagaland.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 330, 332, 333.
        - 52. Fifty-Second Amendment Act, 1985 (Popularly known as Anti-Defection Law)
            - Provided for disqualification of members of Parliament and state legislatures on the ground of defection and added a new Tenth Schedule containing the details.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 101, 102, 190, 191, added Tenth Schedule.
        - 53. Fifty-Third Amendment Act, 1986
            - Made special provisions for Mizoram and fixed the strength of its Assembly at a minimum of 40 members.
            - Amended Articles
                - Added Article 371G.
        - 54. Fifty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1986
            - Increased the salaries of Supreme Court and high court judges and enabled Parliament to change them in the future by an ordinary law.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 125, 221, Second Schedule.
        - 55. Fifty-Fifth Amendment Act, 1986
            - Made special provisions for Arunachal Pradesh and fixed the strength of its Assembly at a minimum of 30 members.
            - Amended Articles
                - Added Article 371F.
        - 56. Fifty-Sixth Amendment Act, 1987
            - Fixed the strength of the Goa Legislative Assembly at a minimum of 30 members.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 239A.
        - 57. Fifty-Seventh Amendment Act, 1987
            - Reserved seats for STs in the legislative assemblies of Arunachal Pradesh, Meghalaya, Mizoram, and Nagaland.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 332.
        - 58. Fifty-Eighth Amendment Act, 1987
            - Provided for an authoritative text of the Constitution in Hindi and gave it legal sanctity.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 394A.
        - 59. Fifty-Ninth Amendment Act, 1988
            - Facilitated the extension of President’s Rule in Punjab up to three years.
            - Provided for the declaration of national emergency in Punjab on the ground of internal disturbance.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Articles 356, 359A.
        - 60. Sixtieth Amendment Act, 1988
            - Increased the ceiling of taxes on professions, trades, callings, and employments from Rs. 250 per annum to Rs. 2,500 per annum.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 276.
        - 61. Sixty-First Amendment Act, 1989
            - Reduced the voting age from 21 years to 18 years for Lok Sabha and state legislative assembly elections.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 326.
        - 62. Sixty-Second Amendment Act, 1989
            - Extended the reservation of seats for the SCs, STs, and special representation for Anglo-Indians in the Lok Sabha and state legislative assemblies for a further period of ten years (i.e., up to 2000).
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 334.
        - 63. Sixty-Third Amendment Act, 1989
            - Repealed the changes introduced by the 59th Amendment Act of 1988 in relation to Punjab, bringing Punjab at par with other states in respect of emergency provisions.
            - Amended Articles
                - Repealed Article 359A, amended Article 356.
        - 64. Sixty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1990
            - Facilitated the extension of President’s Rule in Punjab up to a total period of three years and six months.
            - Amended Articles
                - Amended Article 356.
        - 65. Sixty-Fifth Amendment Act, 1990
            - Provided for the establishment of a multi-member National Commission for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in place of a Special Officer for SCs and STs.

- Appendix VI: Flag Code of India
    - Introduction
        - There is universal affection, respect, and loyalty to the national flag. However, a lack of awareness is often noticed among people and organizations/agencies of the government regarding laws, practices, and conventions that apply to its display. Apart from non-statutory instructions issued by the Government from time to time, the display of the national flag is governed by the Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950, and the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971. The Flag Code of India, 2002, consolidates all such laws, conventions, practices, and instructions for the guidance of all concerned.
        - The Flag Code of India, 2002, is divided into three parts. Part I contains a general description of the national flag. Part II is devoted to the display of the national flag by members of the public, private organizations, educational institutions, etc. Part III relates to the display of the national flag by Central and State Governments and their organizations and agencies.
        - The Flag Code of India, 2002, took effect from January 26, 2002, and superseded the earlier “Flag Code–India.”

    - Part I: General Description of the National Flag
        - 1. The national flag shall be a tricolour panel made up of three rectangular panels or sub-panels of equal widths. The colour of the top panel shall be India saffron (kesari), the bottom panel shall be India green, and the middle panel shall be white, bearing at its centre the design of the Ashoka Chakra in navy blue with 24 equally spaced spokes. The Ashoka Chakra shall preferably be screen-printed or otherwise printed, stenciled, or suitably embroidered and shall be completely visible on both sides of the flag in the centre of the white panel.
        - 2. The national flag shall be made of hand-spun and hand-woven or machine-made cotton, polyester, wool, silk, or khadi bunting.
            - Note: Paragraph 1.2 was amended vide order dated December 30, 2021. Before this amendment, it read: “The national flag of India shall be made of hand-spun and hand-woven wool, cotton, silk, or khadi bunting.”
        - 3. The national flag shall be rectangular in shape. The ratio of the length to the height (width) of the flag shall be 3:2.
        - 4. The standard sizes of the national flag shall be as follows:
            - Flag Size No. 1: 6300 x 4200 mm
            - Flag Size No. 2: 3600 x 2400 mm
            - Flag Size No. 3: 2700 x 1800 mm
            - Flag Size No. 4: 1800 x 1200 mm
            - Flag Size No. 5: 1350 x 900 mm
            - Flag Size No. 6: 900 x 600 mm
            - Flag Size No. 7: 450 x 300 mm
            - Flag Size No. 8: 225 x 150 mm
            - Flag Size No. 9: 150 x 100 mm
        - 5. An appropriate size should be chosen for display. The flags of 450 x 300 mm size are intended for aircraft on VVIP flights, 225 x 150 mm size for motor cars, and 150 x 100 mm size for tables.

    - Part II: Hoisting/Display/Use of National Flag by Members of Public, Private Organizations, Educational Institutions, Etc.
        - Section I
            - 1. There shall be no restriction on the display of the national flag by members of the general public, private organizations, educational institutions, etc., except to the extent provided in the Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950, the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, and any other law enacted on the subject. Keeping in view the provisions of these Acts:
                - (i) The flag shall not be used for commercial purposes in violation of the Emblems and Names (Prevention of Improper Use) Act, 1950.
                - (ii) The flag shall not be dipped in salute to any person or thing.
                - (iii) The flag shall not be flown at half-mast except on occasions when it is flown at half-mast on public buildings in accordance with instructions issued by the Government.
                - (iv) The flag shall not be used as a drapery in any form whatsoever, including private funerals.
                - (v) The flag shall not be used as a portion of a costume or uniform of any description, nor shall it be embroidered or printed upon cushions, handkerchiefs, napkins, or any dress material.
                - (vi) Lettering of any kind shall not be put upon the flag.
                - (vii) The flag shall not be used as a receptacle for receiving, delivering, holding, or carrying anything, except that there shall be no objection to keeping flower petals inside the flag before it is unfurled as part of celebrations on special occasions and on national days like Republic Day and Independence Day.
                - (viii) When used on occasions like the unveiling of a statue, the flag shall be displayed distinctly and separately and shall not be used as a covering for the statue or monument.
                - (ix) The flag shall not be used to cover a speaker’s desk, nor shall it be draped over a speaker’s platform.
                - (x) The flag shall not be intentionally allowed to touch the ground or the floor or trail in water.
                - (xi) The flag shall not be draped over the hood, top, sides, or back of a vehicle, train, boat, or aircraft.
                - (xii) The flag shall not be used as a covering for a building.
                - (xiii) The flag shall not be intentionally displayed with its saffron portion downwards.
            - 2. A member of the public, a private organization, or an educational institution may hoist/display the national flag on all days and occasions, ceremonial or otherwise, consistent with the dignity and honour of the national flag:
                - (i) Whenever the national flag is displayed, it should occupy the position of honour and be distinctly placed.
                - (ii) A damaged or dishevelled flag should not be displayed.
                - (iii) The flag should not be flown from a single masthead simultaneously with any other flag or flags.
                - (iv) The flag should not be flown on any vehicle except in accordance with the provisions contained in Section IX of Part III of this code.
                - (v) When the flag is displayed on a speaker’s platform, it should be flown on the speaker’s right as he faces the audience or flat against the wall, above and behind the speaker.
                - (vi) When the flag is displayed flat and horizontal on a wall, the saffron band should be uppermost, and when displayed vertically, the saffron band shall be on the right with reference to the flag (i.e., left to the person facing the flag).
                - (vii) To the extent possible, the flag should conform to the specifications prescribed in Part I of this code.
                - (viii) No other flag or bunting should be placed higher than, above, or side by side with the national flag; nor should any object, including flowers, garlands, or emblems, be placed on or above the flag-mast from which the flag is flown.
                - (ix) The flag should not be used as a festoon, rosette, or bunting, or in any other manner for decoration.
                - (x) The flag made of paper may be waved by the public on occasions of important national, cultural, and sports events. However, such paper flags should not be discarded or thrown on the ground after the event. As far as possible, they should be disposed of in private, consistent with the dignity of the flag.
                - (xi) Where the flag is displayed in the open or on the house of a member of the public, it may be flown day and night.
                    - Note: Clause (xi) was amended vide order dated July 20, 2022. Before this amendment, it read: “Where the flag is displayed in the open, it should, as far as possible, be flown from sunrise to sunset, irrespective of weather conditions.”
                - (xii) The flag should not be displayed or fastened in any manner that may damage it.
                - (xiii) When the flag is in a damaged or soiled condition, it shall be destroyed as a whole in private, preferably by burning or by any other method consistent with the dignity of the flag.
        - Section II
            - 3. The national flag may be hoisted in educational institutions (schools, colleges, sports camps, scout camps, etc.) to inspire respect for the flag. A model set of instructions for guidance is given below:
                - (i) The school will assemble in an open square formation with pupils forming three sides and the flag-staff at the centre of the fourth side. The headmaster, the pupil leader, and the person unfurling the flag (if other than the headmaster) will stand three paces behind the flag-staff.
                - (ii) The pupils will fall in according to classes and in squads of ten (or another number according to strength). These squads will be arranged one behind the other. The pupil leader of the class will stand to the right of the first row of his class, and the form master will stand three paces behind the last row of his class, towards the middle. The classes will be arranged along the square in order of seniority, with the senior-most class at the right end.
                - (iii) The distance between each row should be at least one pace (30 inches), and the space between form and form should be the same.
                - (iv) When each form or class is ready, the class leader will step forward and salute the selected school pupil leader. As soon as all the forms are ready, the school pupil leader will step forward and salute the headmaster, who will then proceed to hoist the flag.

    - Part III: Display of National Flag by Central and State Governments and Their Organizations and Agencies
        - Section III: Correct Display
            - 8. When the flag is displayed from a staff projecting horizontally or at an angle from a windowsill, balcony, or front of a building, the saffron band shall be at the farther end of the staff.
            - 9. When the flag is displayed flat and horizontal on a wall, the saffron band shall be uppermost, and when displayed vertically, the saffron band shall be to the right with reference to the flag (i.e., to the left of a person facing it).
            - 10. When the flag is displayed on a speaker’s platform, it shall be flown on a staff on the speaker’s right as he faces the audience or flat against the wall above and behind the speaker.
            - 11. When used on occasions like the unveiling of a statue, the flag shall be displayed distinctly and separately.
            - 12. When the flag is displayed alone on a motor car, it shall be flown from a staff, which should be affixed firmly either on the middle front of the bonnet or to the front right side of the car.
            - 13. When the flag is carried in a procession or parade, it shall be either on the marching right (i.e., the flag’s own right) or, if there is a line of other flags, in front of the centre of the line.
        - Section IV: Incorrect Display
            - 14. A damaged or dishevelled flag shall not be displayed.
            - 15. The flag shall not be dipped in salute to any person or thing.
            - 16. No other flag or bunting shall be placed higher than, above, or, except as hereinafter provided, side by side with the national flag; nor shall any object, including flowers, garlands, or emblems, be placed on or above the flag-mast from which the flag is flown.
            - 17. The flag shall not be used as a festoon, rosette, or bunting or in any other manner for decoration.
            - 18. The flag shall not be used to cover a speaker’s desk, nor shall it be draped over a speaker’s platform.
            - 19. The flag shall not be displayed with the saffron portion downwards.
            - 20. The flag shall not be allowed to touch the ground or the floor or trail in water.
            - 21. The flag shall not be displayed or fastened in any manner that may damage it.
        - Section V: Misuse
            - 22. The flag shall not be used as a drapery in any form whatsoever, except in State, military, or Central paramilitary forces’ funerals, as hereinafter provided.
            - 23. The flag shall not be draped over the hood, top, sides, or back of a vehicle, train, or boat.
            - 24. The flag shall not be used or stored in such a manner as may damage or soil it.
            - 25. When the flag is in a damaged or soiled condition, it shall not be cast aside or disrespectfully disposed of but shall be destroyed as a whole in private, preferably by burning or by any other method consistent with the dignity of the flag.
            - 26. The flag shall not be used as a covering for a building.
            - 27. The flag shall not be used as a portion of a costume or uniform of any description, nor shall it be embroidered or printed upon cushions, handkerchiefs, napkins, or boxes.
            - 28. Lettering of any kind shall not be put upon the flag.
            - 29. The flag shall not be used in any form of advertisement, nor shall an advertising sign be fastened to the pole from which the flag is flown.
            - 30. The flag shall not be used as a receptacle for receiving, delivering, holding, or carrying anything, provided that there shall be no objection to keeping flower petals inside the flag before it is unfurled, as part of celebrations on special occasions and on national days like Republic Day and Independence Day.
        - Section VI: Salute
            - 31. During the ceremony of hoisting or lowering the flag or when the flag is passing in a parade or review, all persons present should face the flag and stand at attention. Those present in uniform should render the appropriate salute. When the flag is in a moving column, persons present will stand at attention or salute as the flag passes them. A dignitary may take the salute without a headdress.
        - Section VII: Display with Flags of Other Nations and of United Nations
            - 32. When displayed in a straight line with flags of other countries, the national flag shall be on the extreme right (i.e., if an observer were to stand in the centre of the row of flags facing the audience, the national flag should be to his extreme right).
            - 33. Flags of foreign countries shall proceed from the national flag in alphabetical order based on the English versions of the names of the countries concerned. It is permissible to begin and end the row of flags with the national flag and to include the national flag in the normal country-wise alphabetical order. The national flag shall be hoisted first and lowered last.
            - 34. When flags are flown in an open circle (i.e., in an arc or semicircle), the same procedure as in the preceding clause shall be adopted. When flags are flown in a closed (i.e., complete) circle, the national flag shall mark the beginning of the circle, and the flags of other countries should proceed in a clockwise manner until the last flag is placed next to the national flag. It is not necessary to use separate national flags to mark the beginning and end of the circle. The national flag shall also be included in its alphabetical order in such a closed circle.
            - 35. When the national flag is displayed against a wall with another flag from crossed staffs, the national flag shall be on the right (i.e., the flag’s own right), and its staff shall be in front of the staff of the other flag.
            - 36. When the United Nations’ flag is flown along with the national flag, it can be displayed on either side of the national flag. The general practice is to fly the national flag on the extreme right with reference to the direction it is facing (i.e., the extreme left of an observer facing the masts flying the flags).
            - 37. When the national flag is flown with flags of other countries, the flag masts shall be of equal size. International usage forbids the display of the flag of one nation above that of another nation in time of peace.
            - 38. The national flag shall not be flown from a single masthead simultaneously with any other flag or flags. There shall be separate mastheads for different flags.
        - Section VIII: Display over Public Buildings/Official Residences
            - 39. Normally, the national flag should be flown only on important public buildings such as High Courts, Secretariats, Commissioners’ offices, Collectorates, jails, and offices of District Boards, Municipalities, Zilla Parishads, and departmental/public sector undertakings.
            - 40. In frontier areas, the national flag may be flown on border customs posts, check posts, outposts, and other special places where flying the flag has special significance. It may also be flown on the camp sites of border patrols.
            - 41. The national flag should be flown on the official residences of the President, Vice-President, Governors, and Lieutenant Governors when they are at headquarters and on the building in which they stay during visits to places outside headquarters. The flag flown on the official residence should be brought down as soon as the dignitary leaves headquarters and re-hoisted on that building as he enters the main gate on return. When the dignitary is on a visit outside headquarters, the flag should be hoisted on the building in which he stays as he enters the main gate and brought down as soon as he leaves. However, the flag should be flown from sunrise to sunset on such official residences, irrespective of whether the dignitary is at headquarters, on Republic Day, Independence Day, Mahatma Gandhi’s Birthday, National Week (April 6 to 13, in memory of the martyrs of Jallianwala Bagh), any other specified day of national rejoicing, or, in the case of a State, on the anniversary of its formation.
            - 42. When the President, Vice-President, or Prime Minister visits an institution, the national flag may be flown by the institution as a mark of respect.
            - 43. On the occasion of visits to India by foreign dignitaries, namely, President, Vice-President, Emperor/King or Heir Prince, and Prime Minister, the national flag may be flown along with the flag of the foreign country concerned, in accordance with the rules in Section VII, by private institutions according reception to the visiting dignitaries and on public buildings the foreign dignitaries intend to visit on the day of the visit.
        - Section IX: Display on Motor Cars
            - 44. The privilege of flying the national flag on motor cars is limited to:
                - (1) President
                - (2) Vice-President
                - (3) Governors and Lieutenant Governors
                - (4) Heads of Indian missions/posts abroad in the countries to which they are accredited
                - (5) Prime Minister and other Cabinet Ministers; Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers of the Union; Chief Minister and other Cabinet Ministers of a State or Union Territory; Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers of a State or Union Territory
                - (6) Speaker of the Lok Sabha; Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; Deputy Speaker of the Lok Sabha; Chairmen of Legislative Councils in States; Speakers of Legislative Assemblies in States and Union Territories; Deputy Chairmen of Legislative Councils in States; Deputy Speakers of Legislative Assemblies in States and Union Territories
                - (7) Chief Justice of India; Judges of Supreme Court; Chief Justice of High Courts; Judges of High Courts
            - 45. The dignitaries mentioned in clauses (5) to (7) of Paragraph 3.44 may fly the national flag on their cars whenever they consider it necessary or advisable.
            - 46. When a foreign dignitary travels in a car provided by the Government, the national flag will be flown on the right side of the car, and the flag of the foreign country will be flown on the left side of the car.
        - Section X: Display on Trains/Aircraft
            - 47. When the President travels by special train within the country, the national flag should be flown from the driver’s cab on the side facing the platform of the station from where the train departs. The flag should be flown only when the special train is stationary or when coming into the station where it is going to halt.
            - 48. The national flag will be flown on the aircraft carrying the President, Vice-President, or Prime Minister on a visit to a foreign country. Alongside the national flag, the flag of the country visited should also be flown, but when the aircraft lands in countries en route, the national flags of those countries would be flown instead, as a gesture of courtesy and goodwill.
            - 49. When the President goes on tour within India, the national flag will be displayed on the side by which the President will embark on or disembark from the aircraft.
        - Section XI: Half-Masting
            - 50. In the event of the death of the following dignitaries, the national flag shall be half-masted at the places indicated against each on the day of the death of the dignitary:
                - 1. President, Vice-President, Prime Minister: Throughout India
                - 2. Speaker of the Lok Sabha, Chief Justice of India: Delhi
                - 3. Union Cabinet Minister: Delhi and State Capitals
                - 4. Minister of State or Deputy Minister of the Union: Delhi
                - 5. Governor, Lieutenant Governor, Chief Minister of a State, Chief Minister of a Union Territory: Throughout the State or Union Territory concerned
                - 6. Cabinet Minister in a State: Capital of the State concerned
            - 51. If the intimation of the death of any dignitary is received in the afternoon, the flag shall be half-masted on the following day also at the place or places indicated above, provided the funeral has not taken place before sunrise on that day.
            - 52. On the day of the funeral of a dignitary mentioned above, the flag shall be half-masted at the place where the funeral takes place.
            - 53. If State mourning is to be observed on the death of any dignitary, the flag shall be half-masted throughout the period of mourning throughout India in the case of Union dignitaries and throughout the State or Union Territory concerned in the case of a State or Union Territory dignitary.
            - 54. Half-masting of the flag and, where necessary, observance of State mourning on the death of foreign dignitaries will be governed by special instructions issued by the Ministry of Home Affairs in individual cases.
            - 55. Notwithstanding the above provisions, if a half-mast day coincides with Republic Day, Independence Day, Mahatma Gandhi’s Birthday, National Week (April 6 to 13, in memory of the martyrs of Jallianwala Bagh), any other specified day of national rejoicing, or, in the case of a State, the anniversary of its formation, the flag shall not be flown at half-mast except over the building where the body of the deceased is lying until it has been removed, and the flag shall be raised to the full-mast position after the body has been removed.
            - 56. If mourning is to be observed in a parade or procession where a flag is carried, two streamers of black crepe shall be attached to the spearhead, allowing the streamers to fall naturally. The use of black crepe in such a manner shall be only by an order of the Government.
            - 57. When flown at half-mast, the flag shall be hoisted to the peak for an instant, then lowered to the half-mast position, but before lowering the flag for the day, it shall be raised again to the peak.
                - Note: By half-mast is meant hauling down the flag to one-half the distance between the top and the guy-line and, in the absence of a guy-line, half of the staff.
            - 58. On occasions of State, military, or Central paramilitary forces’ funerals, the flag shall be draped over the bier or coffin with the saffron towards the head of the bier or coffin. The flag shall not be lowered into the grave or burnt in the pyre.
            - 59. In the event of the death of either the Head of State or Head of Government of a foreign country, the Indian mission accredited to that country may fly the national flag at half-mast, even if that event falls on Republic Day, Independence Day, Mahatma Gandhi’s Birthday, National Week (April 6 to 13, in memory of the martyrs of Jallianwala Bagh), or any other specified day of national rejoicing. In the event of the death of any other dignitary of that country, the national flag should not be flown at half-mast by the missions except when local practice or protocol (which should be ascertained from the Dean of the Diplomatic Corps, where necessary) requires that the national flag of a foreign mission in that country also be flown at half-mast.
